answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 10.

answer.text:
Circuit description  
•  M1 is connected as a common-drain (source-follower) NMOS.  
•  M2, whose gate is fixed at the bias voltage Vb, behaves as a saturated NMOS current-sink.  
•  The drain currents of the two devices are identical because the drains are series-connected, so M2 fixes the dc bias current of the follower.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. DC (large-signal) operating point  

Assume both transistors are in saturation and, for the moment, neglect channel-length modulation.

ID2 = ½ k2 (Vb – Vth2)² = I0         (1)     (current set by the bias network)

ID1 = ½ k1 (Vin – Vout – Vth1)² = I0   (2)

Equating (1) and (2) gives the dc transfer:

Vin – Vout – Vth1 = √(k2/k1) ( Vb − Vth2 )         (3)

so that, to first order,

Vout ≈ Vin − VGS1   with VGS1 ≈ √(k2/k1) ( Vb − Vth2 ) + Vth1   (4)

(Body effect can be added in Vth1 if higher accuracy is required.)

Saturation conditions  
M1 : VDD − Vout > VGS1 − Vth1  ⇒ Vin < VDD + Vth1           
M2 : Vout > VGS2 − Vth2 = Vb − Vth2

Hence the output swing must satisfy

Vb − Vth2 < Vout < VDD − VOV1            (5)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal analysis  

Small-signal parameters (at the bias current I0):

gm1 = √(2 k1 I0) ,     ro1 = 1/λ1I0   
ro2 = 1/λ2I0                                (6)

a) Voltage gain  

Applying KCL at the output node:

gm1( vin − vout ) + vout/ro1 + vout/ro2 = 0

Av ≡ vout / vin = gm1 / ( gm1 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )     
    = ( gm1 · (ro1║ro2) ) / ( 1 + gm1 · (ro1║ro2) )      (7)

Because ro1 and ro2 are normally hundreds of kΩ while gm1 is a few mS,  
gm1 (ro1║ro2) ≫ 1 and Av ≃ 0.9–0.99 → the stage is an almost-unity-gain buffer.

b) Output resistance  

Set vin = 0, apply a test voltage vx at the output:

ix = vx ( gm1 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )

Rout = vx / ix = 1 / ( gm1 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )          
    = ( ro1 ║ ro2 ) / ( 1 + gm1 (ro1║ro2) ) ≈ 1/gm1   (tens of Ω).   (8)

c) Input resistance  

The MOS gate is open-circuit: Rin ≈ ∞ (limited only by leakage and any gate-bias network).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. What the current-source load buys you  

• Higher small-signal resistance than a resistor, so the follower gain is closer to 1.  
• The bias current – and therefore gm1 – is independent of Vout, giving predictable small-signal behavior.  
• Better PSRR, because the current is fixed by Vb instead of VDD.  
• Saves voltage headroom compared with a resistor delivering the same current.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Design/usage notes  

1. Choose Vb so that M2 supplies the desired current and still leaves the headroom in (5).  
2. Size M1 so that gm1 (ro1║ro2) ≫ 1 for unity gain and low Rout.  
3. Check that the expected Vin range satisfies the M1 saturation condition in (5).  

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary  
M1–M2 form a source-follower buffered by a constant current sink.  
• DC: Vout ≈ Vin – VGS1 (about one threshold plus over-drive below the input).  
• Small signal: gain slightly < 1, very high input resistance, output resistance of order 1/gm1.  
The stage therefore works well as a low-impedance, level-shifting voltage buffer provided roughly one VGS of headroom is available above and below the output node.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 11(a).

answer.text:
Figure 11(a) is the basic complementary-MOS (CMOS) inverter.  
M2 is a p-channel device (pull-up) whose source is tied to VDD, and M1 is an n-channel device (pull-down) whose source is tied to ground.  Their gates are connected to the input node Vin and their drains are tied together to form the output node Vout.  Below is a complete large–signal (static) and small–signal (dynamic) analysis.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Logic behaviour (truth table)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Vin = 0 V  →  M2 ON (VSG2 = VDD > |VTP|), M1 OFF (VGS1 = 0 < VTN)  
            Vout is pulled up to VDD  ⇒ logic ‘1’.

Vin = VDD  →  M2 OFF (VSG2 = 0),      M1 ON  (VGS1 = VDD > VTN)  
            Vout is pulled down to 0 V ⇒ logic ‘0’.

Thus Vout = ¬Vin; i.e. the circuit is an inverter.  
Because in either dc logic state one of the transistors is OFF, there is (ideally) no direct path from VDD to ground and hence virtually zero static power dissipation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. d.c. transfer characteristic Vout(Vin)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
For the region where both devices conduct (Vin in the vicinity of the switching point) we equate the p-device and n-device drain currents.  Using the long-channel square-law model and assuming both devices are in saturation in the critical region:

Idn = (βn /2) (Vin – VTN)^2  
Idp = (βp /2) (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)^2

Setting Idn = Idp gives the switching (midpoint) voltage VM:

√βn (Vin – VTN) = √βp (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)

VM = (VDD + |VTP| + κ VTN) / (1 + κ) with κ = √(βn / βp)

If the devices are sized so that βp ≈ βn and if |VTP| ≈ VTN (usual in digital design), VM ≈ VDD /2 so the inverter has symmetrical noise margins.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Noise–margin limits VIL and VIH
--------------------------------------------------------------------
VIL and VIH are obtained from the points where the slope of the transfer curve equals –1, i.e. dVout / dVin = –1.  Using the square-law model, one finds:

VIL ≈ VTN + (|VTP| – VTN) √(βp / βn)  
VIH = VDD – VIL

Noise margins:  
NML = VIL – 0, NMH = VDD – VIH.  
With βp ≈ βn both margins are nearly equal and close to VDD/2 – VTN.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Dynamic behaviour (propagation delay)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Let CL be the lumped load capacitance at the output node.

• High-to-low transition (tPHL) – CL is discharged through the ON resistance of M1:  
  Rn ≈ 1 / (βn (VDD – VTN)) → tPHL ≈ Rn CL.

• Low-to-high transition (tPLH) – CL is charged through the ON resistance of M2:  
  Rp ≈ 1 / (βp (VDD – |VTP|)) → tPLH ≈ Rp CL.

Because carrier mobility μn > μp, the p-device is normally given a wider W/L so that βp ≈ βn, making tPHL ≈ tPLH.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Short-circuit (crowbar) current
--------------------------------------------------------------------
During an input transition Vin passes through the range where both transistors are partially ON, producing a momentary current from VDD to ground.  The energy dissipated per transition is

E = CL VDD²  + ∫ ISC(t) VDD dt

but for well-shaped input edges the short-circuit term is usually a few percent of the capacitive term.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Key features of the CMOS inverter
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Rail-to-rail output swing (0 → VDD).  
• High noise margins centred about VDD/2.  
• Ideally zero static power; power is dynamic and ≈ f CL VDD².  
• Output impedance is low in both directions, so the gate can both source and sink current, giving fast transitions.  
• The switching point VM can be centred by sizing (β-ratio) without altering the supply or threshold voltages.

Hence the circuit of Fig. 11(a) is the fundamental building block of all static CMOS logic families, providing full-swing inversion with negligible d.c. power and large noise immunity.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the CMOS inverter and its NMOS pull-down, PMOS pull-up, and logic behavior. The additional analysis is not required for full credit and does not contradict the inverter’s operation.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 11(a).

answer.text:
Figure 11(a) is the elementary complementary-MOS (CMOS) inverter:  

• M2 is a p-channel device whose source is tied to VDD.  
• M1 is an n-channel device whose source is tied to ground (0 V).  
• Both gates are connected to the input node Vin; the drains are connected together to form the output node Vout.

1. DC (static) behaviour  

   a) Vin = 0 V (logic “0”)  
      – VSG(p) = VDD > |VTP| → M2 ON (low resistance).  
      – VGS(n) = 0 V     → M1 OFF.  
      – The only conducting path is from VDD through M2 to Vout, so  
        Vout ≈ VDD (logic “1”).  
      – No direct path from VDD to ground ⇒ essentially zero static power.  

   b) Vin = VDD (logic “1”)  
      – VSG(p) = 0 V → M2 OFF.  
      – VGS(n) = VDD > VTN → M1 ON.  
      – Vout is pulled to ground through M1, so Vout ≈ 0 V (logic “0”).  
      – Again, no DC path from VDD to ground ⇒ Pstatic ≈ 0.  

   c) Vin in the transition region  
      Both transistors conduct partially; the exact value of Vout is found from
         IDn = IDp.  
      Using the long-channel square-law model (neglect channel-length
      modulation) and assuming both devices are in saturation at the switching
      point VM (the voltage where Vout = Vin):

           βn (VM – VTN)² = βp (VDD – VM – |VTP|)²           (1)

      β = μ Cox W/L.  
      Because electron mobility is ≈ 2–3× hole mobility, designers usually make
      the p-device about 2–3× wider so that βp ≈ βn; then

           VM ≈ (VDD + |VTP| + VTN)/2  ≈  VDD/2

      giving a symmetrical voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) and large,
      nearly equal noise margins:  
         NML = VIL, NMH = VDD – VIH ≈ 0.45 VDD or more.

2. Dynamic behaviour (propagation delay and power)

   Let CL be the total capacitance at the output node.

   • High-to-low transition (tPHL)  
     Output is discharged through the n-device:  
        tPHL ≈ (CL · VDD) / ION,n   with ION,n ≈ ½ βn (VDD – VTN)².

   • Low-to-high transition (tPLH)  
     Output is charged through the p-device:  
        tPLH ≈ (CL · VDD) / ION,p   with ION,p ≈ ½ βp (VDD – |VTP|)².

   With βp ≈ βn these two delays are comparable.

   • Power  
     – Static: essentially zero (ideal CMOS).  
     – Dynamic: Pdyn = CL VDD² fSW.  
     – Short-circuit current flows only while Vin is in the transition band
       (both devices partially on) and is usually a few percent of the dynamic
       power for reasonable rise/fall times.

3. Summary of logic function

   Vin   Low  High  
   --------------------------------  
   M2 (pMOS) ON  OFF  
   M1 (nMOS) OFF  ON  
   Vout  High  Low (inverts Vin)

Thus the circuit of Fig. 11(a) is the standard CMOS inverter: it provides a full logic swing (0 → VDD), almost ideal noise immunity, negligible static power dissipation, and balanced propagation delays when the device sizes are chosen so that βp ≈ βn.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 11(a).

answer.text:
Figure 11(a) is nothing more than the textbook CMOS inverter:

• M2 (the upper device) is a p-channel MOSFET; its source is tied to the positive supply VDD, its drain to the output node Vout.  
• M1 (the lower device) is an n-channel MOSFET; its drain is tied to Vout and its source to ground.  
• Both gates are driven by the same input node Vin.

1. DC (logic) behaviour  

   a) Vin ≈ 0 V (logic 0):  
      – M1: VGS,n = 0 < VTH,n  ⇒ M1 is OFF.  
      – M2: VSG,p = VDD > |VTH,p| ⇒ M2 is ON ⇒ Vout is pulled up to VDD.  
      Steady-state current is essentially zero because the pull-down device is off.  
      Result: Vout ≈ VDD (logic 1).

   b) Vin ≈ VDD (logic 1):  
      – M1: VGS,n = VDD > VTH,n ⇒ M1 is ON ⇒ Vout is pulled to ground.  
      – M2: VSG,p = 0 < |VTH,p|  ⇒ M2 is OFF.  
      Again no dc current flows.  
      Result: Vout ≈ 0 V (logic 0).

   c) Intermediate Vin: both transistors conduct, producing a short-lived current from VDD to ground while the output switches.

   Thus the gate realises the NOT function with rail-to-rail output levels and virtually zero static power.

2. Switching (trip) point VM  

   Around the midpoint of the transfer characteristic both transistors are in (velocity-saturated) saturation, so

        Id,n = βn (Vin − VTH,n)²  
        Id,p = βp (VDD − Vin − |VTH,p|)² ,

   and at VM these currents are equal:

        βn (VM − VTH,n)² = βp (VDD − VM − |VTH,p|)² .

   Assuming matched thresholds (|VTH,n| = |VTH,p| = VTH) the solution is

        VM = [√(βn) (VDD − VTH) + √(βp) VTH] / (√(βn) + √(βp)) .

   If the devices are sized so that βn = βp, VM = VDD/2, giving symmetrical noise margins.

3. Noise margins (for βn = βp, equal |VTH|)  

        NMH ≈ NML ≈ VDD/2 − VTH .

4. Other key properties  

   • High input impedance (only gate capacitances are seen by the driver).  
   • Low output impedance when the conducting device is ON.  
   • Dynamic power only: every 0↔1 transition of a load capacitance CL dissipates  
        E = CL VDD²;   Pavg = CL VDD² f if the node toggles each clock cycle.  
   • No body-diode conduction paths exist in the two dc states, so leakage is confined to sub-threshold and junction leakage.

Hence Figure 11(a) is the correct, complementary pull-up / pull-down implementation of a CMOS inverter, offering rail-to-rail signal swing, large noise margins, and zero static power.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 11(b).

answer.text:
Figure 11(b) is what you obtain when you take the two transistors of a normal CMOS inverter and simply interchange their positions without changing anything else (device type, body connection, or the fact that the two gates are tied together).  
At first sight it looks “almost” like an inverter, but a closer look shows that it can never work as a logic gate and that it actually places a permanent short–circuit between the supply rails.

1. Device types and body ties  
   • M1 is an n-channel device that, as usual, has its body (p-substrate) tied to the lowest potential on the chip (ground).  
   • M2 is a p-channel device that, as usual, has its body (n-well) tied to the highest potential (VDD).

2. What the body diodes do  
   Every MOSFET contains two pn-junction diodes between each diffusion (source/drain) and its body.  
   • For the n-MOSFET the diode conducts whenever the diffusion is more than ≈ 0.7 V above the body.  
   • For the p-MOSFET the diode conducts whenever the diffusion is more than ≈ 0.7 V below the body.

   With the devices placed as in Fig. 11(b) those diodes are always forward-biased:

        – Top device (nMOS): its upper diffusion is tied to VDD while its body is at 0 V → diode is forward-biased.  
        – Bottom device (pMOS): its lower diffusion is tied to 0 V while its body is at VDD → diode is forward-biased.

   Consequently a pair of diodes in series is permanently connected between VDD and ground, so a large dc current flows even when the gates are held at any fixed potential.

3. Channel (gate-controlled) conduction  
   Ignoring the diodes for a moment and looking only at the channels:

   • Vin = 0  
     – nMOS (M1) is OFF.  
     – pMOS (M2) is ON, connecting Vout to ground.  
     Output would be low, but the supply is already being shorted through the n-MOS body diode.

   • Vin = VDD  
     – nMOS (M1) is ON, trying to connect Vout to VDD.  
     – pMOS (M2) is OFF.  
     Output would try to go high, but the p-MOS body diode is still providing a return path to ground.

   Even in this “best case” there is still a dc path from VDD to GND (through one forward diode plus the conducting transistor), so the static current is very large and the gate has no valid noise margins.

4. Practical consequences  
   • The circuit never produces a rail-to-rail logic level that is free of contention.  
   • Its static power consumption is essentially VDD / (≈ a few tens of ohms), large enough to destroy an on-chip supply or burn the device.  
   • Because at least one diode is forward-biased at all times, the supply itself would be clamped to about 1.4 V (two diode drops) if the external supply tried to rise higher.

5. Bottom line  
   Swapping the positions of the p- and n-devices while keeping their bodies tied to the usual rails violates the basic CMOS rule that the parasitic junctions must remain reverse-biased.  
   Figure 11(b) therefore is not a functional logic gate at all—it is a permanent short between VDD and ground, and in an actual IC it would immediately lead to catastrophic power-supply currents.

     – The diffusion that is connected to Vout is now a p-to-n-well diode whose
       anode is Vout and whose cathode is VDD.  
   • M2 is an n-MOS device in the p-substrate whose body is at ground.  
     – The diffusion that is connected to Vout is now an n-to-substrate diode whose
       anode is ground and whose cathode is Vout.  

   The output node is therefore clamped by two diodes
       ground ←|-- VD --|- Vout --|<-- VD --|→ VDD
   so that
        0 + VD   ≤ Vout ≤ VDD – VD
   (VD ≈ 0.6–0.8 V for silicon).

2. Static operation

   (a) Vin = 0 (logic ‘0’)  
       – PMOS (M1) turns ​on​ and tries to pull Vout to VDD.  
       – NMOS (M2) is ​off​, but its body diode is forward as soon as  
         Vout > VD.  
       – Result: Vout rises only to ≈ VDD–VD and a DC current flows
         VDD → PMOS channel → diode of M2 → GND.

   (b) Vin = VDD (logic ‘1’)  
       – NMOS (M2) turns ​on​ and tries to pull Vout to ground.  
       – PMOS (M1) is ​off​, but its body diode is forward as soon as  
         Vout < VDD–VD.  
       – Result: Vout sinks only to ≈ VD and a DC current flows
         VDD → diode of M1 → NMOS channel → GND.

   (c) Intermediate Vin  
       Both transistors conduct and at least one of the two diodes is
       forward-biased, so there is still a low-impedance path from VDD
       to ground.

3. Consequences

   • Output never reaches the rails (logic-0 ≈ 0.7 V, logic-1 ≈ VDD–0.7 V).  
   • The gate has practically zero noise margin and cannot reliably drive a
     normal CMOS input.  
   • A ​static​ current flows in every logic state, so the power
     dissipation is large even when the input is not switching.  
   • During switching all four devices (two channels and two diodes) can
     conduct simultaneously, further increasing the short-circuit current.

Hence the network of Fig. 11(b) is ​not​ a valid CMOS inverter; it violates both
CMOS design rules:

1. The output must swing rail-to-rail.  
2. There must be no DC path between VDD and ground in a stable logic
   state.

If we simply reconnect the upper diffusion of the p-MOS to be its source
(VDD) and the lower diffusion of the n-MOS to be its source (ground) we
recover the proper inverter of Fig. 11(a).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 11(b).

answer.text:
Figure 11(b) looks very similar to the well-known complementary CMOS inverter in Fig. 11(a):  

• the two transistors are in series between VDD and ground,  
• their gates are tied together and driven by Vin, and  
• the common drain node is the output Vout.  

The crucial difference is that in Fig. 11(b) the **upper device (M1) is an n-channel MOSFET and the lower device (M2) is a p-channel MOSFET** – the opposite of what is required.  
(You can recognise the type of a MOSFET from the little substrate arrow or the absence / presence of the inversion bubble on the gate.).

Below is a step-by-step dc analysis that shows why this “malformed” inverter cannot be used in digital logic.

--------------------------------------------------
1. Device operation for the two logic input values
--------------------------------------------------

a) Vin = 0 V (‘0’)  
   • M1 (nMOS): VGS = 0 V  →  OFF  
   • M2 (pMOS): VSG = 0 V  →  OFF  
   Result: BOTH TRANSISTORS ARE OFF → Vout is left high-impedance (undefined).  
   No valid logic ‘1’ is produced.

b) Vin = VDD (‘1’)  
   • M1 (nMOS): VGS = VDD – Vout  
     – As soon as Vout is lower than VDD – VTn, M1 turns ON and behaves as a
       source follower (pulls Vout up but can never raise it above VDD – VTn).  
   • M2 (pMOS): VSG = 0 V – VDD = –VDD  
     – |VSG| > |VTp|, so M2 is **strongly ON**, trying to pull Vout DOWN.  

   Consequently both devices conduct simultaneously, creating a direct current
   path from VDD to ground.  The static operating point is found from
   Ipull-up = Ipull-down.  If the two devices are roughly the same strength, one
   obtains

        Vout ≈ VTn     (a few hundred millivolts above ground)

   The gate never delivers a valid logic ‘0’ (0 V).

--------------------------------------------------
2. Voltage transfer characteristic (simplified)
--------------------------------------------------

For Vin < VTn       : both devices off … Vout floats (undefined)  
For Vin ≈ VTn … VDD : both devices on   … Vout ≈ Vin – VTn  
Slope ≈ +1 ➔ voltage gain never exceeds unity (no regeneration).  

The transfer curve therefore never reaches the rails and the noise-margin
bands of a digital inverter are essentially zero.

--------------------------------------------------
3. Static power dissipation
--------------------------------------------------

Because the two MOSFETs conduct at the same time whenever Vin ≳ VTn,
a large short-circuit current flows continuously:

        IDS ≈ (βn/2)(Vin–VTn)^2     (assuming both are in saturation)  

At Vin = VDD the dc power is roughly

        Pstatic ≈ ½ βn (VDD–VTn)^2 · VDD           (very large)

whereas the correctly wired CMOS inverter of Fig. 11(a) consumes **zero**
static power in either logic state.

--------------------------------------------------
4. Summary of the “malformed” inverter’s behaviour
--------------------------------------------------

• It produces neither a valid logic ‘1’ nor a valid logic ‘0’.  
• The small-signal gain is < 1, so it cannot regenerate logic levels.  
• It exhibits a direct dc path between the supply rails for most input
  voltages, wasting a great deal of power.  
• Noise margins are practically non-existent.  
• Hence the gate cannot be used in reliable digital circuitry; it only
  behaves as a poorly-defined analogue voltage divider.

The analysis demonstrates why a **complementary arrangement (PMOS pull-up,
NMOS pull-down)**, as in Fig. 11(a), is essential for a proper CMOS inverter.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 12.

answer.text:
Figure-12 is the classical “common-source amplifier with a diode-connected load”.  
M1 is the amplifying device, M2 (whose gate is shorted to its drain) plays the role of an active, MOS-implemented “resistor”.

Notation  
βi = μn Cox (W/L)i ,  Vt = threshold voltage (assume identical for the two devices),  
λ = channel–length-modulation coefficient (set to 0 in the first pass).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Large-signal (DC) operation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Vin < Vt ⟹ M1 is cut off → ID ≃ 0.  
 With no current through M2, Vout is pulled to the supply, Vout ≃ VDD.

• Vin ≥ Vt ⟹ Both transistors conduct and the same current I flows through
  the series stack.

  – M2 is always in saturation because it is diode connected:
       VDS2 = VGS2  and VDS2  ≥  VGS2 – Vt   (always true)

  – Region A – both devices saturated  
        I = ½β1 (Vin – Vt)^2 = ½β2 (VDD – Vout – Vt)^2
        ⇒ Vout = VDD – Vt – √(β1/β2) (Vin – Vt)

        Valid while Vout ≥ Vin – Vt  (otherwise M1 leaves saturation).

  – Region B – M1 in triode, M2 saturated (occurs at high Vin)  
        I = β1[(Vin – Vt)Vout – ½Vout^2] = ½β2 (VDD – Vout – Vt)^2

        The above equation can be solved for Vout(Vin) if a complete
        transfer characteristic is needed.

  In digital language the circuit behaves as an NMOS inverter whose
  low-level cannot fall below about Vt; the transition point (Vin = Vout)
  lies in the “both-saturated” region as long as the sizes are chosen so
  that √(β1/β2) is not too large.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal (mid-band) analysis  
   (bias in the “both-saturated” region, I = IDC)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
gm1 = 2I/(Vin – Vt) , gm2 = 2I/(VDD – Vout – Vt)

At the output node (AC ground at the top because the supply is bypassed)

   gm1 vin – (gm2 + gds2 + gds1) vout = 0

   ⇒ Av = vout / vin = – gm1 / (gm2 + gds1 + gds2)
                    ≃ – gm1 / gm2  (gm2 ≫ gds terms)

If λ ≃ 0, gm ∝ √β, so

   |Av| ≃ √(β1/β2)

Hence the voltage gain is set by the device-size ratio; making M1 wide
and/or M2 narrow increases the magnitude of the gain.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Input, output impedances and pole
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Rin  ≈  ∞  (open MOS gate)

Rout = 1 / (gm2 + gds1 + gds2) ≃ 1/gm2  (≈ a few kΩ for µ-A bias currents)

Dominant pole:  fp ≈ 1 / [2π Cload Rout]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Summary of properties
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• Only n-type devices are required; the stage biases itself automatically.  
• Mid-band gain  |Av| ≃ √(β1/β2) (= –gm1/gm2 when channel-length
  modulation is neglected).  
• Output cannot swing to 0 V; the minimum value is ≈ Vt + VDS(sat) of M2,
  so the logic “0” level is degraded.  
• Useful as a simple linear amplifier or as a pedagogical NMOS inverter,
  but not competitive with a CMOS inverter for rail-to-rail digital logic.

This completes the large-signal and small-signal analysis of the
common-source amplifier with a diode-connected MOS load shown in Fig. 12.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 12.

answer.text:
Figure-12 is the simplest MOS common-source stage that uses an “active” (i.e. transistor) load:  
an n-channel transistor M1 driven at the gate by the input voltage and a p-channel transistor M2 whose gate is shorted to its drain (diode connection) and tied to the output node.  
The circuit is therefore often called

• a common-source amplifier with a diode-connected (PMOS) load, or  
• a one-transistor inverter with a depletion / active load.

Below the circuit is analysed first in large-signal (DC) sense and then in small-signal
terms.  Channel-length-modulation (λ = 0) is ignored unless stated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Large-signal (DC) analysis
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Regions of operation

a) Vin  ≤  VTHn – NMOS is OFF  
 ID1 = 0 ⟹ ID2 = 0, therefore no current flows through M2 and  
  Vout ≃ VDD.  
 (The PMOS is cut off because VSG2 = VDD – Vout < |VTHp|.)

b) Vin  ≥  VTHn – NMOS begins to conduct.  
 The diode–connected PMOS always satisfies VSD2 = VSG2, therefore as soon as it
conducts it is automatically in saturation because  

        VSD2 ≥ VSG2 – |VTHp| → saturation condition is met.

 For the range of Vin in which M1 is *also* in saturation

        VDS1 = Vout ≥ VGS1 – VTHn        [required for sat. of M1]

 both devices conduct the *same* drain current ID and we can write

        ID = (kn/2)(Vin – VTHn)² = (kp/2)(VSG2 – |VTHp|)²

 where  
  kn = μnCox(W/L)n and kp = μpCox(W/L)p.

 With VSG2 = VDD – Vout the above equality gives a simple linear
relationship between the two node voltages

               √kn (Vin – VTHn) = √kp (VDD – Vout – |VTHp|)

         ⇒ Vout = VDD – |VTHp| – (√kn / √kp)(Vin – VTHn)   (1)

 Equation (1) is valid as long as

         Vin ≥ VTHn           (turn-on of M1)  
         Vout ≥ 0  and Vout ≥ Vin – VTHn  (saturation of M1)

 If Vin is increased further, Vout given by (1) would eventually try to go
negative; the real circuit of course limits Vout to ≈0 V and M1
enters the triode region while the current continues to rise.

 Thus, in large signal the stage behaves qualitatively like an inverter:

• Low Vin → High Vout (≈ VDD)  
• High Vin → Low Vout (≈ a few hundred mV above ground)

 but the low level cannot reach exactly 0 V unless |VTHp| ≃ VTHn.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal analysis (both transistors in saturation)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Small-signal parameters

 gm1 = ∂ID/∂VGS1 = kn (Vin – VTHn)  
 gm2 = ∂ID/∂VSG2 = kp (VDD – Vout – |VTHp|)

 A diode-connected MOSFET presents to the node a resistance

   rL = 1 / gm2

Small-signal equivalent circuit

 • Gate of M1 is the input; its small-signal resistance is ∞.  
 • Output node sees –gm1·vgs1 current source of M1 in parallel with
  rL and, if λ ≠ 0, the output resistances ro1 || ro2.

Neglecting λ (ro → ∞) the voltage gain is

  Av = vout / vin = – gm1 · rL = – gm1 / gm2

 Using the definition of gm’s and the equality of the drain currents we find

  gm1 / gm2 = √kn / √kp     (2)

Hence, in the ideal long-channel device the small-signal gain is

  Av = – √kn / √kp

Remarks

1. The magnitude of the gain is independent of the bias current; it depends
   only on the device transconductance parameters (i.e. widths, lengths and
   carrier mobilities).  
   For equal-sized, equal-mobility devices kn ≃ kp and |Av| ≃ 1.  
   To obtain |Av| > 1 the PMOS is normally made *smaller* (kp < kn), or
   the NMOS is made larger.

2. Including ro-effects, the gain becomes

  Av = – gm1 ( rL || ro1 || ro2 )  
   ≈ – gm1 / ( gm2 + 1/ro1 + 1/ro2 )

   so finite ro’s reduce |Av| somewhat.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Summary of important points
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• M2 is diode-connected; therefore it is *always* in saturation once it
  conducts.  
• With both devices in saturation the DC transfer characteristic is the
  straight line of eqn. (1).  
• Small-signal gain (long-channel) is –√(kn/kp); in practice it is seldom
  much larger than –3 to –4 unless the width ratio is made extreme.  
• Input resistance is infinite; output resistance is roughly 1/gm2 in
  parallel with the two ro’s.  
• The circuit can serve as a very compact analog voltage amplifier
  (actually a trans-resistance with built-in load) or, in digital work, as a
  ratioed inverter.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 12.

answer.text:
We treat M1 as an n-channel MOSFET used in the common-source configuration and M2 as a p-channel MOSFET whose gate is shorted to its drain (a “diode-connected” load).  Long–channel square-law devices and negligible channel-length modulation are assumed.

1. DC operating regions  

   a. Vin  <  VTN  
      •  M1 is OFF → ID = 0  
      •  M2 therefore also carries no current → Vout = VDD  
      •  The stage is an open circuit; small-signal gain ≈ 0.  

   b. Vin  ≥  VTN  
      •  M1 turns ON and the same current must flow through M2.  
      •  Because M2 is diode-connected, VSD2 = VSG2 ; consequently VSD2 = VSG2 > |VTP| so M2 is always in saturation.  
      •  If the value of Vout obtained below satisfies  
           Vout ≥ Vin – VTN                                   
        then M1 is also in saturation, and this is the region in which the amplifier is intended to operate.

2. DC transfer characteristic (Vin → Vout)  

   The drain current of the two transistors must be equal:  

        ID = ½ βn (Vin – VTN)^2               (M1 in sat.)  
        ID = ½ βp (VSG2 – |VTP|)^2            (M2 in sat.)  

   with  VSG2 = VDD – Vout.  Equating the two expressions,

        ½ βn (Vin – VTN)^2  =  ½ βp [ (VDD – Vout) – |VTP| ]^2

        ⇒  VDD – Vout  =  |VTP| + √(βn / βp) (Vin – VTN)

        ⇒  Vout = VDD – |VTP| – √(βn/βp) (Vin – VTN)        for Vin ≥ VTN

   The characteristic is therefore piece-wise linear: a horizontal segment at VDD followed by a line of negative slope −√(βn/βp).

   Limit for both devices to remain saturated  

        Vout ≥ Vin – VTN  (condition for M1)  

     Substitute Vout from the previous expression and solve for Vin:

        Vin ≤ VTN + (VDD – |VTP|) / [1 + √(βn/βp)]

     This gives the allowable Vin (and correspondingly Vout) signal swing.

3. Small-signal parameters  

        gm1 = ∂ID/∂VGS1 = √(2 βn ID)  
        gm2 = ∂ID/∂VSG2 = √(2 βp ID)

   The diode-connected M2 behaves as a small-signal resistor  
        rL = 1 / gm2  

   Small-signal voltage gain  

        Av = − gm1 · rL = − gm1 / gm2 = − √(βn / βp)

   •  If devices are laid out so that βn = βp  → |Av| ≈ 1.  
   •  A larger magnitude of gain is obtained by enlarging M1 (increasing gm1) and/or shrinking M2 (decreasing gm2).

4. Input and output resistances  

   •  Rin (at the gate of M1) is ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
   •  Rout (looking into the drain of M2) is rL ∥ ro2.  With channel-length modulation neglected, ro2 → ∞ and Rout ≈ rL = 1/gm2.

5. Summary of main results  

   Vout (dc):   Vout = VDD                                   for Vin ≤ VTN  
                Vout = VDD – |VTP| – √(βn/βp)(Vin – VTN)     up to Vin(max) above  

   Small-signal gain:        Av = – gm1 / gm2 = – √(βn / βp)  

   Allowable Vin range (both devices saturated):  
                VTN  ≤ Vin ≤  VTN + (VDD – |VTP|)/(1 + √(βn/βp))

   Within this region the circuit behaves as an inverting voltage amplifier whose gain is set only by the ratio of the two transconductances (i.e. essentially by the W/L ratio of the two transistors).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 13.

answer.text:
Below is a compact “data-sheet” style analysis of the two–transistor stage of Fig. 13.  
(We assume a normal CMOS process, VDD is the positive supply, the sources of the
p-channel devices are the more‐positive terminals, body ties are implicit, and both
transistors are biased in saturation unless otherwise noted.)

1.  Topology identification  
    • M2 is a p-channel device: its source is at VDD and its gate is driven by Vin.  
    • M1 is an n-channel device: its source is at ground.  
    • The drain of M2 and the drain-plus-gate of M1 are shorted, so M1 is
      diode-connected.  
    • The output is the common drain node “Vout”.

    With a “live” pMOS on top and a diode-connected nMOS
    load on the bottom, the stage is often called a gm/gm amplifier because its
    small-signal gain is the ratio of two transconductances.

2.  dc operating point (square-law, λ≈0)

        ID  = ID1 = ID2
        ID1 = ½ kn(W/L)1 (Vout – Vtn)^2                    (nMOS, VGS1 = VDS1 = Vout)
        ID2 = ½ kp(W/L)2 (VDD – Vin – |Vtp|)^2             (pMOS, VSG2 = VDD – Vin)

        ⇒  kn(W/L)1 (Vout – Vtn)^2  =  kp(W/L)2 (VDD – Vin – |Vtp|)^2.

    From this relation one can solve Vout as a function of Vin, or size the two
    transistors so that the quiescent current meets a specification.

    Saturation requirements  

        Vout  ≥ VDSsat1  = Vov1                             (keeps M1 in sat.)
        Vin   ≥ Vout + |Vtp|                               (keeps M2 in sat.)

3.  Small-signal model

        gm1 = √(2 kn(W/L)1 ID)      (nMOS, diode-connected)
        gm2 = √(2 kp(W/L)2 ID)      (pMOS, common-source)

        ro1 , ro2  » 1/gm1   ⇒  ignore for a first-order gain estimate.

    • M1 appears as a resistor  r1 ≈ 1/gm1  from Vout to ground.  
    • The incremental drain current contributed by M2 is

            id2 = – gm2 · vin          (because  υsg2 = –vin and pMOS gm is positive).

    Node equation at Vout (currents leaving node toward ground taken positive):

            (– gm2 vin)  +  gm1 vout  =  0

            ⇒   vout =  (gm2 / gm1) · vin

        Small-signal voltage gain      Av  ≡  vout / vin  =  + gm2 / gm1.

        Because Av is a ratio of two gms it

        • can be set accurately by sizing (W/L) ratios,  
        • tracks process, temperature, and bias variations,  
        • needs no large resistors.

4.  Impedance & bandwidth

        Input resistance        Rin  ≈ ∞   (MOS gate).  
        Output resistance       Rout ≈ 1/gm1 ‖ ro1 ‖ ro2  ≈ 1/gm1.  
        3-dB pole              fp ≈ 1 / [2π (Rout) · Cload].

5.  Qualitative behaviour

    • When Vin rises, |VSG2| falls → ID tries to decrease.  
    • The only available path for the current is through the diode-connected M1,
      so the node voltage Vout must fall to reduce its conductance and keep
      ID1=ID2.  
    • Because the sign of the incremental transfer is positive (gain ≈ +gm2/gm1),
      the stage is non-inverting.  Large gains (10-20) are readily obtained
      without cascoding or high-valued resistors by choosing gm2 » gm1.

6.  Limitations and design hints

    • Ensure both devices stay in saturation over the entire input range using the
      inequalities in Sec. 2.  
    • ro effects, body effect, mobility degradation and channel-length modulation
      reduce the gain slightly:

            Av ≈ gm2 / (gm1 + gmb1 + gm2λ2/gm1 …).

    • For higher gain use cascode loads or mirror the M1 current into a larger
      load transistor, but at the price of head-room.

The circuit of Fig. 13 therefore realises a simple, single-ended gm/gm amplifier
whose small-signal gain is set by the ratio of the transconductances of two
MOSFETs, granting resistor-less, process-robust gain with very small silicon
area.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 13.

answer.text:
Figure 13 is the simplest possible “gm / gm” CMOS voltage amplifier:  
– the input-transconductance element is the p-channel device M2, whose gate is the signal input Vin;  
– the load is not a resistor but another transconductance element, the n-channel device M1, which is wired as a diode (gate shorted to drain, i.e. to the output node).  
Because both the numerator and the denominator of the gain expression are transconductances, the voltage gain is the ratio gmp / gmn – hence the name gm / gm amplifier.

1. DC operating point (square-law model, channel-length-modulation neglected)

   M2 (p-MOS, source at VDD, drain at Vout, gate Vin):

      ID = (½)βp (VSG – |VTP|)²  
         = (½)βp (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)²                               (1)

   M1 (n-MOS, gate = drain = Vout, source at 0 V):

      ID = (½)βn (VGS – VTN)²  
         = (½)βn (Vout – VTN)²                                      (2)

   Equating (1) and (2) gives the transfer characteristic

      Vout = VTN + √(βp/βn)·(VDD – Vin – |VTP|)                    (3)

   – It is a straight line with negative slope √(βp/βn).  
   – Because Vout must remain between the two saturation boundaries
        Vout ≥ VTN                      (M1 in saturation)  
        VDD – Vout ≥ VDD – Vin – |VTP|  (M2 in saturation)  
     the legal Vin range is only a few hundred millivolts below VDD.

2. Small-signal gain (ro → ∞ first)

   Small-signal drain currents

      id2 = gmp(–vin)                 (gate excitation of M2)  
      id1 = gmn(+vout)                (gate = drain connection of M1)

   KCL at Vout:    id1 + id2 = 0 ⇒ gmn·vout – gmp·vin = 0

      Av = vout / vin = – gmp / gmn = – √(βp/βn)                    (4)

   Taking typical mobility ratio μn / μp ≈ 2–3 (and equal L), |Av| is only
   about 1.3–1.7; i.e. the stage by itself has modest gain but is very
   compact and free of explicit resistors.

   With channel-length modulation included,

      Av ≈ – gmp / (gmn + go1 + go2)                                (5)

   which lowers the magnitude further.

3. Salient properties

   • No passive resistors: the “load” is the controlled current of M1
     (1 / gmn acts as the effective resistance).  
   • Gain accuracy depends primarily on device-dimension ratios, not on
     absolute values – convenient in IC processes.  
   • Because the allowable Vin range is close to the positive rail and the
     attainable gain is small, the topology is usually employed inside
     larger, differential, or gain-boosted structures rather than as a
     stand-alone high-gain stage.

In summary, the circuit of Figure 13 converts Vin to a current through M2
(gmp·Vin), which is then converted back to a voltage by the diode-connected
transconductor M1.  The resulting mid-band gain is the ratio of the two
transconductances:

  |Av| ≈ gmp / gmn = √(βp/βn) (≈ 1.5 for typical CMOS processes).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 13.

answer.text:
The two devices of Fig-13 are p-channel MOSFETs that have been stacked “source-to-drain”.  
M2 (at the top) is the signal-controlled element; M1 (at the bottom) is biased at a
constant gate voltage and behaves like a second, fixed transconductance.  
Because the same drain current flows through both devices, their two
i = g m  · v relations can be equated and the node voltage Vout becomes the ratio (gm /gm),
hence the name “gm /gm amplifier”.

1. DC (large-signal) behaviour

 Rout ≈ (g​m2+g​mb2) r​o1 r​o2  ≈  g​m2 r​o1 r​o2.                (5)

approximation

 Rout ≃ gm2 ro1 ro2  ≈  ro1 (1 + gm2 ro2).

answers.question: How do we ensure that M2 is in saturation in Figure 14?

answer.text:
For an n-channel cascode device the saturation condition is  

 VDS2 ≥ VGS2 – VTH2 .

For the transistor M2 in Fig. 14

 VDS2 = VDD – VX  
 VGS2 = Vb2 – VX .

Insert these values:

 VDD – VX ≥ (Vb2 – VX) – VTH2  
       ⇓ the node-voltage VX cancels out  
 VDD ≥ Vb2 – VTH2 .                                (1)

Therefore the voltage at node X does not affect the condition; M2 is guaranteed to be in saturation as long as its gate-bias voltage Vb2 is at least one threshold voltage below VDD.

Practical procedure:

1. Choose the overdrive (VOV2 = VGS2 – VTH2, typically 0.1–0.2 V) required to carry the desired current.
2. Set the gate-bias voltage  
  Vb2 = VTH2 + VOV2 + VX(desired).
3. Make sure that (1) is satisfied, i.e. Vb2 ≤ VDD – VTH2.  
   With VDD ≈ 1.8 V and VTH ≈ 0.4 V, picking Vb2 around 0.8–1.0 V easily fulfills the requirement.

Because VDD is the highest node in the circuit and Vb2 is chosen at least VTH below it, M2 will remain in saturation for any expected swing of the intermediate node X or the output node.

For an n-MOS transistor the saturation (long-channel) condition is  

  VDS2 ≥ VGS2 – Vth2    (1)

In Fig. 14  

  VDS2 = VDD – VX  
  VGS2 = VB2 – VX

Insert these two expressions into (1):

  VDD – VX ≥ VB2 – VX – Vth2  
  ⟹ VDD ≥ VB2 – Vth2  (2)

Equation (2) no longer contains VX; it says that as long as the gate-bias VB2 is at least one threshold voltage below the supply, the transistor cannot leave saturation, no matter how VX moves.

Practical design rule  
1. Generate VB2 so that it is roughly VDSsat (≈ VOV) below VDD:

  VB2 ≈ VDD – VDSsat2

   (A replica/diode-connected transistor that carries the same current is often used for this bias.)

2. The resulting source voltage of M2 will be

  VX ≈ VB2 – VGS2 ≈ VDD – VDSsat2 – VGS2

   leaving about VDSsat2 of head-room between the drain (VDD) and the source (VX).

Because VDSsat2 ≈ VOV2 is typically 0.1–0.3 V, the inequality in (2) is easily satisfied, and M2 remains firmly in saturation over the entire operating range.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 15.

answer.text:
Small-signal quantities  
gm1 , ro1 : transconductance and intrinsic output resistance of the input device M1  
gm2 , ro2 : transconductance and intrinsic output resistance of the cascode device M2  
ro3 : small-signal resistance of the bias current source I1 (→ ∞ for an “ideal” source)

I. Large-signal (bias) conditions  
1. M1 must be in saturation:       VX ≥ VGS1 – VT1  (= VDSsat1)  
2. M2 must be in saturation:       Vout – VX ≥ VGS2 – VT2  (= VDSsat2)  
With Vb1 tied to the gate of M2 we usually choose

 VX ≃ VGS1 – VT1 + 100…200 mV   (keeps M1 firmly in saturation)  
 Vb1 = VX + VT2                                 (because VGS2 = Vb1 – VX)

For a given tail current I1 the drain currents of M1 and M2 are therefore fixed and both transistors remain in saturation over the intended output-swing range.

II. Small-signal model  

1. Input resistance  
The gate of M1 is an MOS gate ⇒ Rin ≈ ∞ (only Cgs1 is seen).

2. Output resistance of the cascoded pair  
Apply a test current iT at the output node (drain of M2) and find the resulting vout.

KCL at node X (the M1 drain / M2 source):

 gm1 vin + vx/ro1 + (vx–vout)/ro2 + gm2 vx = 0  (1)

KCL at the output node with the test current:

 iT + gm2 vx + (vout–vx)/ro2 = 0        (2)

Solve (1)–(2) for vout / iT with vin = 0 (to determine rout):

 rout = vout/iT = ro2 + (1 + gm2 ro2) ro1 ≈ gm2 ro2 ro1  if  gm2 ro2 ≫ 1

If the current source is realised with a MOS transistor its finite resistance
appears in parallel:

 Rout,total = ( ro2 + (1+gm2 ro2) ro1 )  ‖  ro3 ≈ (gm2 ro2 ro1) ‖ ro3

3. Voltage gain  
With no small-signal current flowing into the ideal source (ro3 → ∞) the only small-signal current that reaches the output node is −gm1 vin.  Hence

 Av = vout / vin = – gm1 · rout

  ≈ – gm1 · gm2 · ro1 · ro2  (if gm2 ro2 ≫ 1 and ro3 → ∞)

Compared with a simple common-source stage (Av,CS = –gm1 ro1) the gain is
increased by the factor gm2 ro2.

Example  
gm1 = gm2 = 1 mA/V, ro1 = ro2 = 100 kΩ ⇒ gm2 ro2 = 100

 Single-transistor CS: Av ≈ –1 mA/V · 100 kΩ = –100  
 Cascoded stage:   Av ≈ –(1 mA/V)(1 mA/V)(100 kΩ)(100 kΩ) = –10 000

III. Advantages of the cascode gain stage  
• Very large voltage gain (because Rout is boosted by gm2 ro2)  
• M1 sees a nearly constant drain voltage ⇒ much smaller Miller (Cgd) effect ⇒ wider bandwidth at the input node.  
• Precise control of VX through Vb1 guarantees that M1 always stays in saturation.

Summary  
Input resistance : ≈ ∞  
Output resistance : Rout ≈ gm2 ro2 ro1 ( ‖ ro3 if the current source is not ideal)  
Voltage gain     : Av ≈ –gm1 Rout ≈ –gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2 (largest when ro3 ≫ Rout)

Those expressions completely characterise the small-signal behaviour of the NMOS cascode gain stage shown in Fig. 15.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 15.

answer.text:
Solution outline

1.  What the circuit is  
    • M1 is a common-source input transistor that converts the small-signal input voltage vin to a drain current gm1·vin.  
    • M2 is wired as a common-gate (cascode) device.  Its gate is fixed at the bias voltage Vb1 so that its small-signal gate node is an ac ground.  
    • I1 is a (ideally) high-output-resistance current source that forces a dc current I1 through the cascade and at the same time plays the rôle of the load.

2.  Large–signal (bias) relations  
    With an ideal current source the dc drain current of the two MOSFETs is identical and equal to I1.  
    Let VOV1, VOV2 be the overdrive voltages of M1 and M2.  In saturation

          Vx   =  VGS1  =  VTH1 + VOV1                  (node X voltage)
          VGS2 =  Vb1 – Vx  =  VOV2 + VTH2

    Saturation constraints

          M1 :  VDS1 = Vx > VOV1                       ( ≈ VOV1 in practice)
          M2 :  VDS2 = Vout – Vx ≥ VOV2
          ⇒ Vout(min) ≃ VOV1 + VOV2

    These two inequalities dictate the choice of the bias Vb1 and the lowest supply voltage that still keeps both transistors in saturation.

3.  Small-signal equivalent

             ro3                ro2                 ro1
        VDD ────◀───• vout ───▶───• vx ───▶───• 0
                     |gm2·(–vx)      |gm1·vin
                     |               |
           (a.c.     ▼               ▼
            ground)  ⏐              ground

    Where  
        gm1 , ro1  – small-signal transconductance and output resistance of M1  
        gm2 , ro2  – the same for M2  
        ro3        – small-signal resistance of the current source I1 (∞ for an ideal source)

4.  Output resistance (seen at vout)  
    Driving the input to zero (vin = 0) and applying a test voltage vx to node vout gives

          Rout = ro2 + (gm2·ro2)·ro1          ( ro3 → ∞ )
                ≃ gm2 · ro1 · ro2            if gm2 ro2 ≫ 1

    Hence the cascode boosts the output resistance roughly by the factor gm2 ro2.

5.  Mid-band voltage gain  
    The small-signal gain is

          Av = vout / vin =  – gm1 · Rout

    For the ideal current source case

          Av ≃ – gm1 · gm2 · ro1 · ro2      (gm2 ro2 ≫ 1)

    i.e. the gain is approximately the product of the intrinsic gains of M1 and M2:

          |Av| ≃ (gm1 ro1) · (gm2 ro2) = A0,1 · A0,2

    Even with modern short-channel devices whose intrinsic gain is moderate (10-30), the squared dependence lets the cascode reach gains of several hundred to a few thousand.

6.  Other small-signal quantities  
    • Input resistance Rin ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
    • Voltage gain from vin to the intermediate node (node X):

          Ax = vx / vin ≃ – gm1 / (gm2 + 1/ro2) ≈ – gm1 / gm2    (gm2 ro2 ≫ 1)

      Therefore the swing at node X is small, which greatly reduces the Miller multiplication of Cgd1 and extends the high-frequency bandwidth of the stage.

7.  Design insight  
    • A high gm2 and a large ro2 are both beneficial; the cascade translates them into a very large output resistance.  
    • Because the minimum output swing is VOV1 + VOV2, the price paid for high gain is head-room (voltage).  
    • The current-source load should possess as large an ro3 as practical; a finite ro3 simply appears in parallel with Rout and lowers the gain.

In summary: The two-transistor NMOS cascode exploits the common-gate action of M2 to hold M1’s drain nearly fixed, thereby turning the intrinsic gain of each transistor into a product and yielding

          Av  ≈  –gm1·gm2·ro1·ro2        (ideal load)

with an output resistance

          Rout ≈ gm2·ro2·ro1

and only a small intermediate-node swing, all at the cost of roughly two overdrive voltages of head-room.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-source NMOS and M2 as the common-gate NMOS cascode, and gives the equivalent ideal-load gain, satisfying the golden full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 15.

answer.text:
The circuit in Fig-15 is the classical NMOS cascode gain stage:

• M1 is the “amplifying” common-source transistor.  
• M2 is a common-gate (cascode) device whose only job is to keep the drain of M1 at an almost fixed a.c. potential, thereby multiplying the small-signal output resistance.  
• I1 is an (ideally) infinite-output-resistance current source that biases the stack with the d.c. current I1.

Below the symbol βx means gdx = 1/rox.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
1.  d.c. bias conditions
────────────────────────────────────────────────
ID1 = ID2 = I1    (series devices)

Let Vx be the M1 drain / M2 source node.

M1 in saturation  Vx ≥ VGS1 – VTH1 = VOV1  
M2 in saturation  Vout – Vx ≥ VGS2 – VTH2 = VOV2  
Choose Vb1 so that VGS2 = VOV2 :

 Vb1 ≃ Vx + VOV2  (with a few 10 mV margin)

The minimum supply is therefore

 VDD(min) ≈ VOV1 + VOV2 + VDS(sat) of the current source.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Small-signal model
────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Replace I1 with an open circuit.  
• Gate of M2 (Vb1) is an a.c. ground.  
• Small-signal parameters:

 gm1, gm2  transconductances  
 ro1, ro2  output resistances (gd conductances β1, β2)

Unknown node voltages: vx and vo.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Relationship between vx and vo
────────────────────────────────────────────────
KCL at the output node (no external load):

 –gm2 vx + β2 (vo – vx) = 0

⇒ vo = vx (1 + gm2 ro2)   (1)

Because gm2 ro2 ≫ 1, vx is only a small fraction of vo; node X is
effectively a.c. grounded.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Voltage gain Av  = vo / vin
────────────────────────────────────────────────
KCL at node X (include M1):

(β1 + β2 + gm2) vx – β2 vo + gm1 vin = 0

Use Eq-(1) to suppress vx and solve for vo/vin:

Av = –gm1 ro1 – gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2   (2)

For usual long-channel numbers gm2 ro2 ≫ 1, the first term is negligible:

 Av ≈ –gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2   (≈ –Ai1 × Ai2)

The gain is roughly the product of the intrinsic gains of M1 and M2, so
several tens of thousands are easily obtained with modest device sizes.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
5.  Output resistance Rout
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Set vin = 0, inject a test current It at the drain and solve:

 Rout = ro2 + gm2 ro1 ro2  ≈ gm2 ro1 ro2  (3)

Thus the cascode multiplies the “plain” ro2 by ≈ gm2 ro1.

────────────────────────────────────────────────
6.  Other small-signal properties
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Input resistance Rin → ∞ (MOS gate)  
Overall transconductance (io / vin) Gm ≈ gm1  
Impedance of node X Rx ≈ 1/gm2   (a few hundred Ω)

────────────────────────────────────────────────
7.  Frequency behaviour
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Because Rx is small, the Miller multiplication of M1’s Cgd is
suppressed by the factor 1/(1+gm2 ro2); therefore the pole associated
with Cgd1 is pushed to a much higher frequency than in a simple
common-source stage with the same gain.  The dominant capacitance at the
output is Cdb2 (and any load).

────────────────────────────────────────────────
8.  Summary
────────────────────────────────────────────────
• High gain: |Av| ≈ gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2  
• High output resistance: Rout ≈ gm2 ro1 ro2  
• Wide bandwidth because node X is a.c. grounded.  
• Price paid: extra voltage head-room (VOV1 + VOV2) and an additional
  bias voltage Vb1.

That completes the analysis of the NMOS cascode gain stage of Fig-15.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-source NMOS and M2 as the common-gate NMOS cascode, and gives the equivalent ideal-load gain −gm1·ro1(1+gm2·ro2). The claim that node X is effectively AC-grounded is imprecise for an ideal current-source load, but the golden solution’s full-credit rule applies.

answers.question: Is the circuit of Figure 16 a cascode structure?

answer.text:
Yes.  
Transistor M1 is used as the common-source (CS) input device: its gate is the signal node Vin, its source is at ground, and its drain is the internal node that connects to the source of M2.  
Transistor M2 has its gate held at a fixed bias voltage Vb1, so it operates as a common-gate (CG) device. Because its gate is fixed, M2 keeps the drain of M1 at an almost constant voltage, greatly increasing the small-signal output resistance seen looking into M1’s drain and suppressing the Miller effect.  

The cascade of a CS stage followed immediately by a CG stage is precisely what the word “cascode” denotes.  
The resistor RD is simply the load; whether the load is a resistor, a current-source transistor, or something else does not change the fact that the pair M1–M2 forms a cascode.

So the circuit of Figure 16 is a cascode amplifier (more specifically, an NMOS simple cascode with a resistive load).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Incorrectly calls the circuit a cascode and misidentifies M1 as an NMOS common-source device; M1 is a PMOS source follower, so the structure lacks cascode resistance boosting.

answers.question: Is the circuit of Figure 16 a cascode structure?

answer.text:
Yes.  
A cascode consists of

1. A “driving” device used in the common-source / common-emitter configuration (it converts the input voltage into a signal current), and  
2. A second device placed directly on top of it and operated in the common-gate / common-base mode, biased with a fixed gate (or base) voltage so that it keeps the first device’s drain (or collector) voltage nearly constant and presents a very large incremental resistance to the load.

In Figure 16

• M1 is the common-source device: Vin is applied to its gate, its source is at ground, and the signal current appears at its drain.  
• M2 is the common-gate (cascode) device: its gate is held at the dc bias Vb1, so for small-signal purposes its gate is an ac ground.

M1 is a common-source (CS) input transistor; M2 is stacked on top of it with its gate fixed at the dc bias voltage Vb1, so M2 operates as a common-gate (CG) device.  
A CS transistor whose drain is “shielded” from the output node by a CG transistor is exactly what is meant by a cascode.  

For the pair to behave as a cascode the following must hold.

1. Both MOSFETs are biased in saturation:  
   VDS1 ≥ VOV1 and VDS2 ≥ VOV2.  
2. The gate of the upper device is not the signal node (it is tied to a constant Vb1).  
3. The source of the upper device is the drain of the lower one, so the drain of M1 sees almost a constant voltage (≈ Vb1 – VTH2).  

Replacing the usual current-source load by a resistor RD simply limits the attainable gain; it does not change the fact that the topology is a CS-CG cascode.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect only “inflates’’ a capacitance when the two terminals of that capacitance see a large signal gain with respect to each other.  

Common-source / common-emitter stage  
• Cgd (MOS) or Ccb (BJT) is connected between the input node (gate/base) and the drain/collector.  
• The small-signal gain from input to that node is approximately −gm ro (often ­10…−100).  
• The effective input capacitance therefore becomes Ceff ≃ Cgd(1+|Av|), many times larger than the physical device capacitance, and the -3 dB frequency is pushed downward.

Cascode (common-source followed by common-gate, or common-emitter followed by common-base)  

1. The cascode transistor keeps the first device’s drain/collector at almost constant a-c voltage.  
   • Its gate/base is at a-c ground.  
   • Its very low small-signal impedance looking into the source/emitter forces the drain/collector of the input transistor to move only a few millivolts, even while the top node (the real output) swings volts.  

2. Consequently the gain from the input gate/base to that drain/collector node is only |Av1| ≈ 0…1 instead of |Av| ≫ 1.  

3. The multiplication factor of the gate–drain (or base–collector) capacitance is therefore  
   Ceff ≃ Cgd(1+|Av1|) ≈ 1–2 × Cgd  
   rather than tens of times Cgd.  

4. The large overall gain of the cascode (product of the two stages) now appears between the intermediate node and the final output node, but there is no capacitance tying that high-gain pair of nodes back to the input, so no Miller multiplication is produced there.

In short: the cascode “shields’’ the input device’s reverse transfer capacitance by holding the node on the other side of that capacitor at a nearly fixed a-c potential, so the Miller effect—capacitance multiplication and the attendant bandwidth loss—is largely eliminated.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies that the cascode’s low-impedance intermediate node reduces the gain across Cgd and its multiplication to roughly 1–2×. However, it overstates the effect by describing the node as nearly fixed and the Miller effect as largely eliminated; the gain is typically about −1, so the effect is reduced, not negligible.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
Miller effect = capacitance-multiplication that occurs when a capacitance is connected between two nodes whose small-signal voltages differ by a high gain.  
For the gate–drain (Cgd) capacitance of a common-source MOS or the base–collector (Cμ) capacitance of a BJT:

Effective input capacitance Cin ≃ Cgd · (1 + |Av,gate→drain|)

1. Common-source / common-emitter stage  
   • Av,gate→drain ≈ –gm·Rload (tens to hundreds)  
   • Cin is therefore multiplied by the same factor → large Miller capacitance, dominant pole is at a low frequency.

2. Cascode stage (common-source transistor stacked with a common-gate / common-base transistor)  
   • The common-gate device keeps the drain of the input device at a nearly constant AC voltage (it sits at a low impedance).  
   • Small-signal gain from the gate to that drain node is therefore ≈ 0…1 instead of tens.  
        Av,gate→drain ≈ –gm1·ro1 ‖ 1/gm2  ≈ –1 (often even lower in magnitude).  
   • Multiplication factor 1 + |Av| ≈ 1 → Cgd contributes almost its physical value only.  
   • Thus the input node “sees” much smaller capacitance, the dominant pole is pushed to a higher frequency, and bandwidth improves.

In short: In a cascode the drain (or collector) voltage of the input transistor does not swing much, so the voltage across Cgd (or Cμ) is small; without a large voltage gain across that capacitor there is almost no Miller multiplication, making the Miller effect much less pronounced.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies that the common-gate device makes the input transistor’s drain a low-impedance node, reducing its voltage gain and Miller effect. However, it overstates the reduction: the gain is roughly −1, so Cgd is multiplied by about 2, not nearly 1 or its physical value alone.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
Miller multiplication only happens when there is a large signal gain across the capacitance that connects the input node to some other node.  
For a single common-source / common-emitter stage that capacitance is Cgd (or Cbc).  
Its input-to-output gain is large and negative (A ≈ –gm RD, often several-tens), so the
capacitance that the signal source has to drive is

Cin ≈ Cgs + (1 + |A|) Cgd        ← “Miller-expanded” Cgd

Cascode connection:

1. The first transistor (Q1) is still used in common-source/common-emitter mode.  
2. Its drain/collector, however, is tied to the SOURCE/EMITTER of a second transistor (Q2) that is biased as a common-gate/common-base stage.  
3. The small-signal resistance looking into the source/emitter of Q2 is about 1/gm2 – a few tens of ohms – therefore the drain/collector of Q1 is a very low-impedance node.  
4. Because of that low impedance the voltage that can appear at the drain/collector of Q1 is only a small fraction of the voltage applied at its gate/base:

  |Av (gate→drain of Q1)| = |vd1 / vg1| ≈ gm1 / (gm2 + …) ≲ 1   (often 0.1 … 0.3)

5. The Miller factor is now

  1 + |Av| ≈ 1 … 2   (instead of 1 … 50 or more).

Therefore the input sees almost the physical Cgd/Cbc itself; the large Miller enlargement that dominates a single-stage amplifier disappears. In other words, the common-gate/common-base transistor “holds” the collector/drain of the input transistor almost at a.c. ground, isolating the input node from the large voltage swings that occur at the final output.  
With the Miller effect suppressed, the cascode offers a much higher input pole frequency and hence a wider bandwidth than a simple common-source/common-emitter stage.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance M1-drain/M2-source node and the reduced gain across Cgd, giving a Miller factor of roughly 1–2 rather than the full-stage gain. Its claims that the node is nearly AC ground and the gain is often 0.1–0.3 overstate the suppression, but the golden solution treats this as a minor flaw.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
Circuit description  
• M2 is an n-channel device whose gate is permanently biased at Vb1.  
  The signal is applied to M2’s source, so the device operates in common-gate
configuration.  
• M1 is a p-channel transistor that furnishes an active (current-source) load.  
  Its gate is tied to the fixed bias voltage Vb2, therefore vgs1 = 0 in small-signal
analysis and the only small-signal element that appears for M1 is r​o1.  
• The output node is the common drain of the two transistors.

1. DC (large-signal) bias  
Assuming both devices are in saturation, the bias current I flowing through the
stack is

 I = ½ k′p(W/L)1 (VSG1–|Vtp|)²(1+λpVSD1)
  = ½ k′n(W/L)2 (VGS2–Vtn)²(1+λnVDS2)

with  
 VSG1 = VDD – Vb2 , VSD1 = VDD – Vout  
 VGS2 = Vb1 – Vin , VDS2 = Vout – Vin

The chosen values of Vb1 and Vb2 (together with the device sizes) set the quiescent
current I and the dc output voltage.

Saturation conditions  
 M1 : VSD1 > VSG1 – |Vtp|  ⇒ Vout < VDD – VOV1  
 M2 : VDS2 > VOV2     ⇒ Vout > Vin + VOV2

Allowed small-signal swing
 Vin + VOV2 < Vout < VDD – VOV1.

2. Small-signal model  
With all dc supplies ac-grounded:

• M1 → only r​o1 from node Vout to ground ( g​m1·vgs1 = 0 ).  
• M2 →  g​m2vgs2 current source from drain to source, r​o2
between drain and source.  
 vgs2 = –vin  (because the gate is ac-ground and the source is the input).

KCL at Vout (currents leaving the node taken positive)

 vout/r​o1 + (vout – vin)/r​o2  – g​m2vin = 0

Voltage gain  

 Av ≡ vout/vin = (g​m2 + 1/r​o2)/(1/r​o1 + 1/r​o2)  
  ≈ g​m2(r​o1 || r​o2)  if g​m2r​o2 ≫ 1

The gain is positive because the stage is non-inverting (typical of a common-gate
amplifier).

3. Input resistance  
Current entering the source node is

 iin = g​m2vin + (vin – vout)/r​o2 .

With vout expressed from the KCL above, the incremental input resistance is

 Rin = vin/iin ≈ 1/g​m2  (if g​m2r​o2 ≫ 1)

Body effect, when the body is not tied to the gate, adds g​mb so that

 Rin ≈ 1/(g​m2 + g​mb).

Because g​m is large, Rin is only a few tens of ohms—one of the reasons common-gate
stages are attractive as wide-band input buffers.

4. Output resistance  
Looking into the drain we see the two output resistances in parallel:

 Rout ≈ r​o1 || r​o2.

When λ ≠ 0 this can be tens of kilohms, so the product g​m2·Rout yields a gain of
10-30 V/V (20-30 dB) with minimum device effort.

Summary  
The circuit in Fig. 17 is a common-gate n-MOS amplifier that uses a p-MOS active
load.  It provides

• Low input resistance: Rin ≈ 1/g​m2  
• High, positive voltage gain: Av ≈ g​m2(r​o1 || r​o2)  
• High output resistance: Rout ≈ r​o1 || r​o2  
• Output swing bounded by Vin + VOV2 < Vout < VDD – VOV1.

Such a topology is often employed as the first stage of wide-band amplifiers or
as the input leg of a differential pair when a very small source impedance has
to be sensed.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
Circuit description  
• M1 is a PMOS whose source is tied to VDD and whose drain is the output node.  
  Its gate is at the d.c. bias Vb2, so it behaves as a saturated PMOS current-source load.  
• M2 is an NMOS placed underneath M1.  
  – Gate voltage = Vb1 (a d.c. bias, therefore an a.c. ground).  
  – Signal Vin is applied to the source terminal.  
  – Drain is the output node.  
Hence the stage is a common-gate NMOS amplifier with a PMOS active load.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. D.C. (large-signal) bias equations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assuming long-channel devices and ignoring channel-length modulation for the moment

ID1 = ½ kp(W/L)1 (VSG1 – |VTP|)²        with VSG1 = VDD – Vb2  
ID2 = ½ kn(W/L)2 (VGS2 – VTN)²          with VGS2 = Vb1 – Vin

The branch current is the same through both devices:

ID = ID1 = ID2                                           (1)

Equation (1) fixes the quiescent current once Vb1 , Vb2 , device sizes and Vin (bias value) are chosen.

Saturation (strong-inversion) conditions

For M2 (NMOS) :     VDS2 ≥ VGS2 – VTN  →  Vout  – Vin ≥  Vb1 – Vin – VTN
                                                   →  Vout ≥ Vb1 – VTN          (2)

For M1 (PMOS):      VSD1 ≥ VSG1 – |VTP| →  VDD – Vout ≥ VDD – Vb2 – |VTP|
                                                   →  Vout ≤ Vb2 + |VTP|        (3)

The bias point must satisfy (2) and (3) simultaneously.

Input swing limits  
To keep M2 on:     Vb1 – Vin > VTN  (Vin must stay at least one threshold below Vb1).  
To keep M2 saturated as Vin changes, Vout must continue to obey (2); this normally
sets the positive input-swing limit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Small-signal (mid-band) model
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Small-signal parameters at the bias current ID

gm2 = 2ID / (VGS2 – VTN)           (NMOS transconductance)  
ro2 ≃ 1/(λn ID)                    (NMOS output resistance)  
gm1 = 2ID / (VSG1 – |VTP|)         (PMOS transconductance – gate is a.c. grounded)  
ro1 ≃ 1/(λp ID)                    (PMOS output resistance)

Because vgs1 = 0 in small signal, gm1 does not contribute; M1 appears only as ro1.

Nodal KCL at the output (downward currents taken positive)

iro1  +  iM2  = 0  
vout/ro1  +  [ –gm2 vin + vout/ro2 ]  = 0

Solve for vout/vin:

Av ≡ vout / vin =  gm2 (ro1 ∥ ro2)          (positive, non-inverting)    (4)

If ro1 ≫ ro2 (PMOS is a “good” current source) Av ≈ gm2 ro2.  
If ro2 ≫ ro1  Av ≈ gm2 ro1.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Input and output impedances
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Input seen at the source of a common-gate device:

iin = gm2 vin  + (vin – vout)/ro2  ≅ gm2 vin      (because ro2 ≫ 1/gm2)  
Rin = vin / iin  ≅ 1/gm2                             (low, a few tens of Ω)

Output resistance with the input port open:

Rout = ro1 ∥ ro2                                    (high, ≈ 50 kΩ–100 kΩ)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Qualitative behaviour
--------------------------------------------------------------------
• A positive increment on Vin decreases vgs2, hence Id2.  
  With less current pulled through M1, Vout rises – the stage therefore has
  a positive (non-inverting) gain, characteristic of a common-gate amplifier.  

• High gain is achieved because gm2 is multiplied by the large load resistance
  ro1 ∥ ro2 while the input impedance is only 1/gm2, giving good current-to-voltage
  conversion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Voltage gain (mid-band)        Av ≈ + gm2 (ro1 ∥ ro2)  
Input resistance               Rin ≈ 1 / gm2 (very low)  
Output resistance              Rout ≈ ro1 ∥ ro2 (high)  
Bias constraints               Vb1 – Vin > VTN,  Vb1 – VTN ≤ Vout ≤ Vb2 + |VTP|

The circuit is therefore a common-gate amplifier with an active PMOS load that
provides a large signal-handling range and a sizeable, positive mid-band gain.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS with PMOS current-source load, places Vin at M2’s source, and gives the non-inverting gain ≈ gm2(ro1 ∥ ro2) and low input resistance. Its approximate Rin treatment is explicitly acceptable under the full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
Circuit description  
• M2 is an n-channel MOSFET whose gate is the signal input.  
   Its source is tied to the fixed bias Vb1, so M2 operates as a common-source
   device.  
• M1 is a p-channel MOSFET whose gate is biased at the constant voltage Vb2 and
   whose source is connected to VDD.  
   With its gate and source both at ac ground, M1 behaves as a
   current-source load whose small-signal contribution is only its output
   resistance ro1.  
• The drains of the two transistors are shorted; that node is the output.  
   Therefore the stage is a common-source n-MOS amplifier that is loaded by the
   small-signal resistance of a saturated p-MOS transistor.

I.  Large–signal (DC) operation  

Assuming both devices are biased in saturation,

ID = (½)kn(W/L)2 (Vin – Vthn)²(1+λn(Vout – Vb1))        (1)  
ID = (½)kp(W/L)1 (VDD – Vb2 – |Vthp|)²(1+λp(VDD – Vout)) (2)

The quiescent current is obtained by equating (1) and (2).
Saturation limits for the output node:

• For M2 (nMOS)      VDS2 = Vout – Vb1 ≥ VGS2 – Vthn  ⇒  Vout ≥ Vin – Vthn  
• For M1 (pMOS)      VSD1 = VDD – Vout ≥ VSG1 – |Vthp| ⇒  Vout ≤ Vb2 + |Vthp|

Hence the signal swing has to stay inside  
             Vin – Vthn  ≤  Vout  ≤  Vb2 + |Vthp|.

II.  Small-signal model  

Let  
gm2 = ∂ID/∂VGS2 evaluated at the bias point (nMOS)  
ro2 = 1/gds2 = 1/(λnID)  
ro1 = 1/gds1 = 1/(λpID)  

Because VGS1 is fixed, gmp does not appear in the small-signal model of M1; the
device contributes only ro1 that connects Vout to ac ground.

Small-signal currents at node Vout (currents defined as flowing out of the node):

• Through M2 :      id2 = gm2 vin  +  gds2 vout  
• Through M1 :      id1 = gds1 vout  

KCL:  id1 + (–id2) = 0  ⇒  gm2 vin + (gds1 + gds2) vout = 0

Voltage gain  

   Av = vout / vin = – gm2 / (gds1 + gds2)
        = – gm2 (ro1 || ro2)

Thus the gain is set by the n-device transconductance times the parallel
combination of the two output resistances.  Because the p-device’s gm is not
used, the achievable gain is modest (typically one digit to a few-tens, unless
very long devices are employed).

Input and output resistances  

• Rin ≅ ∞ (MOS gate)  
• Rout = ro1 || ro2 = 1/(gds1 + gds2)

III.  Observations  

1. If channel-length modulation were neglected (λ = 0 ⇒ ro → ∞) the gain would
   collapse to zero: the stage relies on the finite ro of the stacked
   transistors to generate voltage gain.  
2. Bias point is fixed by Vb1, Vb2, and the chosen VIN(Q).  Once the desired
   ID is set through Vb2, VIN must be adjusted so that (1)=(2).  
3. The structure is useful when only a moderate gain is required and a single
   p-type device is available as an active load; for large gain a mirrored
   (diode-connected) load or a cascoded topology is preferred.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit of Figure 18 have?

answer.text:
Each independent node that can store charge contributes one pole.  
In the small-signal picture there are three such nodes:

1. The input/gate node of M1 – RS in series with (CGS + CGD) produces one pole.  
2. The main output node (M1 drain / M2 source) – the resistance looking into the node together with CDB, CGD and the portion of CGD2 referred to this node gives a second pole.  
3. The cascode-drain node (M2 drain) – the large ro of the load in combination with CDB2 forms a third pole.

Thus the circuit of Figure 18 is a 3-pole network.

2. The drain of M₁ / source of M₂ (Vout node), whose impedance is the small-signal resistance looking into the cascode device and whose capacitance is CDB + CGD (from M₁) + CGD2 (from M₂).

All other terminals (the gate of M₂ and the drain of M₂) are fixed at ac ground, so the capacitors connected to them do not introduce additional dynamic nodes.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Because the two nMOS transistors are identical, driven by the same gate-voltage Vin and placed in series, the stack can be viewed as a “composite” nMOS whose channel has simply been made twice as long.  The argument is identical to the way two equal resistors in series behave like one resistor of twice the value.

1.  Drain current in the linear (triode) region  
    Id ≃ μn Cox W/L · [(VGS–VTH)·VDS – ½ VDS²]  
    When the two devices are placed one above the other, the total VDS (= Vout) is shared almost equally (neglecting body effect).  Each device therefore carries the same current as the single device would carry if its channel length were 2 L; i.e.  

       Id,stack ≃ μn Cox W/(2L) · [(VGS–VTH)·VDS – ½ VDS²]  
       → βstack = βsingle/2  (β = μn Cox W/L)

2.  Saturation region  
    Id,sat = ½ β (VGS–VTH)² (1+λ VDS)  

    a)  With both transistors in saturation the same result is obtained:  
        • Each of the two devices sees roughly half the channel-length modulation, so   
          λstack ≃ λ/2 (because λ ∝ 1/L).  
        • Since the current is limited by the weakest device, the effective β is again β/2.  

    b)  The mid-node VX rises to whatever value is necessary to equalise the currents of the two devices.  Ignoring second-order body-effect terms, VX settles close to the small difference between the intrinsic VTH of the bottom device and the body-raised VTH of the upper one (a few hundred millivolts), and is practically independent of Vin once both transistors are in saturation.  Thus the stack behaves as a cascode: the lower device sees a nearly fixed VDS and the overall small-signal output resistance roughly doubles.

3.  Small-signal parameters  
    gm,stack  =  ∂Id/∂VGS  ≃  gm/2  
    ro,stack  =  1/(λstack Id)  ≃  2 ro  

    Hence the intrinsic gain (gm ro) of the composite device is approximately unchanged, but the current for a given over-drive is one-half of a single device while the output resistance doubles.

4.  Practical consequence for the circuit of Fig. 19  
    •  The resistor RD and the series pair form a common-source amplifier.  
    •  Replacing the two-transistor stack by a single nMOS whose length is 2 L (or equivalently whose β is halved and λ is halved) gives the same dc transfer curve and the same small-signal behaviour as long as both devices operate in saturation.  
    •  Any difference that remains is dominated by the body effect in the upper transistor, which typically alters the bias point by only a small amount.

Therefore the series connection of the two equal nMOS transistors in Fig. 19 can be analysed, to first order, as one long-channel nMOS whose channel length is twice as large.

However, the analysis materially misstates the operating regions: the lower device is in triode and the upper is saturated, not both saturated as a cascode, and the equal-VDS and resulting equivalence claims are invalid.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Because the two n-channel transistors M1 and M2 are placed one above the other and their gates are hard-wired together, the pair carries exactly the same drain current at every instant.  In long-channel theory this allows the two devices to be replaced by one equivalent device whose channel is simply the sum of the individual channel pieces.

Assumptions  
• Long-channel devices, μn and Cox uniform  
• Channel-length modulation, velocity-saturation and body-effect ignored (separate well, or γ ≈ 0)  
• Both transistors are identical: width W, length L  

1. Small-signal (ohmic) point of view  
For VDS << (VGS – VTH) the channel behaves like a resistor  

 I = μn Cox (W/L) (VGS – VTH) VDS  

Hence the incremental channel resistance is  

 rch = 1 / [ μn Cox (W/L)(VGS – VTH) ]  

Placing two identical resistors in series doubles the resistance; therefore the pair is equivalent to a single transistor whose channel length is 2 L (the resistance is proportional to L/W).

2. Saturation (large-signal) point of view  
For each device in saturation  

 ID = ½ μn Cox (W/L) (VGS – VTH)² ≡ ½ β (VGS – VTH)² , β = μn Cox W/L  

Replacing L → 2 L gives  

 ID(series) = ½ μn Cox [W/(2 L)] (VGS – VTH)² = ½ (β/2) (VGS – VTH)²  

i.e. the β (or k-factor) of the series combination is exactly one-half of a single device’s β.  In general, N identical transistors in series give βeq = β / N, which is the same as keeping W fixed and replacing L by N L.

3. Consequences for the inverter of Fig. 19  

• Pull-down strength: Because β is halved, the pull-down network is half as strong as a single NMOS of the same width.  
• Switching point: The reduced pull-down drive shifts the VM (logic threshold) upward toward VDD.  
• VOL and delay: The output low level rises and the fall-time increases unless the width of each transistor is doubled to restore the original β.  
• Noise margins: NMH increases, NML decreases in the same proportion.

4. Practical corrections  

If the bodies of both devices share the global n-well (standard CMOS), M2 sees a positive VSB when current flows; its threshold rises and the effective β falls still further, so the pair is a little weaker than the ideal “2 L” prediction.  Designers therefore widen the transistors slightly more than the 2 : 1 rule when accurate pull-down strength is required.

Summary  
Two identical NMOS transistors that are stacked in series with their gates tied together behave, to first order, like a single NMOS device whose channel length is the sum of the individual lengths.  Equivalently, the effective β (or W/L) of the stack is the single-device β divided by the number of transistors in the stack.
