The extra inverter and body-effect discussion is not needed, but does not undermine the essential conclusion.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Circuit description  
The two identical n-channel MOSFETs M1 and M2 are placed in series between the output node and ground, while their gates are shorted to the input node Vin. A load resistor RD pulls the output node toward the supply VDD. The chain therefore forms the pull-down device of a simple inverter/amplifier, but that pull-down path is itself made of two equal transistors that carry exactly the same drain current.

Because the devices are identical and the same current must flow through both of them, the series connection can be viewed – to first order – as one MOS transistor whose channel is twice as long as that of either device.  We therefore speak of an “effective long-channel” device of length 2L (width W is unchanged).

1. Large-signal (DC) behaviour

Ignoring body-effect and channel-length modulation and assuming long-channel square-law devices:

• If Vin < VTH   →   both transistors are cut off, no current flows, Vout ≈ VDD.  
• VTH < Vin < 2VTH → M1 begins to conduct, its drain (node X) rises, so VGS2 = Vin­–VX is still < VTH and M2 is off – almost no current flows, Vout still ≈ VDD.  
• Vin ≥ 2VTH → both devices turn on and the output can be pulled low.

In the region where both devices conduct, both of them operate with small VDS (each sees roughly half of the total drain-to-source voltage), i.e. in the linear region, so the Id of each device is

 Id = μnCox (W/L)[(VGS – VTH) VDS – ½VDS²]

If the drop across every MOSFET is small enough to let us neglect the quadratic term, the current is proportional to VDS / (W/L). Two such “resistances” in series simply add.  Re-writing the sum in the same form gives exactly the expression of one MOSFET whose channel length is 2L:

 Id(stack) ≈ μnCox (W/2L) (Vin – 2VTH) VDS(total)

Thus the conduction of the stack equals that of a single transistor whose length has doubled (or, in the language of digital design, as if the width had been divided by two).

When Vin is high enough to drive both transistors deep into inversion, each device may even reach saturation, but because the bottom device has the larger overdrive, it usually enters saturation first while the upper device remains in the linear region.  Even in that case the overall current still follows the same 1/(2L) law within a few per-cent accuracy.

2. Effective threshold and ON current

Because the upper device’s source is allowed to rise, it never receives the full gate over-drive that the lower device sees.  A convenient way to summarise this “stack effect” is to say that the chain behaves as if its threshold voltage had doubled:

 Id(stack) ≈ (½)kn (W/L)(Vin – 2VTH)²  (for Vin ≥ 2VTH, both transistors saturated)

where kn ≡ μnCoxW/L.  Compared with a single transistor driven by the same Vin the ON current is roughly divided by two.

3. Small-signal parameters (around a bias point where both devices conduct)

Equivalent long-channel length Leff = 2L →  

• gm(eff) = ∂Id/∂Vin = (μnCox W/2L) (Vin – 2VTH)  
    = ½ · gm(single-device)  

• ro(eff) ≈ 2 · ro(single-device)  (because λ ∝ 1/L)  

Hence the voltage gain of the common-source stage

 Av ≈ – gm(eff) · (RD || ro(eff))  

is about one half of what the same stage would deliver with only one transistor in the pull-down path (all other things being equal).

4. Sub-threshold / leakage view

In weak inversion the drain current of one MOSFET follows

 Id ≈ I0 exp[(Vin – VTH)/(nVT)]

For two identical series devices that share the same gate voltage the approximate current becomes

 Id(stack) ≈ I0 exp[(Vin – 2VTH)/(nVT)]

so the effective threshold is indeed doubled and, for a given Vin, the leakage is exponentially smaller.  This is why the “stack effect” is widely used in digital logic to reduce static leakage.

Summary  
When two identical nMOS transistors whose gates are tied together are placed in series, the combination can be modelled very accurately (for most analogue or digital calculations) as one transistor whose channel length is the sum of the individual lengths.  As a consequence:

• The conduction (ON) current is roughly half that of a single device.  
• The effective small-signal transconductance is halved, the output resistance is doubled.  
• The apparent threshold voltage of the chain is about 2 VTH, leading to a strong reduction of sub-threshold leakage.  
These results fully characterise the circuit of Fig. 19 and explain why series-connected MOSFETs are sometimes called an “effective long-channel” device.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the common-gate series NMOS pair and clearly concludes that its effective channel length is approximately 2L, which the golden solution explicitly treats as sufficient for full credit.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
The two transistors do exactly what their connections suggest:

• M1 is a common-drain (source-follower) stage: its drain is tied to the a.c. ground (VDD) and the signal is taken from its source.

• M2 is a common-gate stage: its gate is held at the fixed bias VB, the signal is applied to its source, and the output is taken at its drain through the load resistor RD.

The follower gives the composite circuit an almost infinite input resistance, while the common-gate device gives the voltage gain.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Small-signal analysis (λ = 0, no body effect)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Define the small-signal quantities

vin  – input voltage at the gate of M1  
vs   – small-signal voltage at the common source node  
vo   – small-signal output voltage  
gm1 , gm2 – transconductances of M1 and M2  

1. Currents of the two devices  
   M1 :  id1 = gm1 (vin – vs)                       (1)  
   M2 :  id2 = –gm2 vs                              (2)

   (The minus sign appears because the gate of M2 is at a.c. ground,
   so vgs2 = –vs.)

2. KCL at the source node  
   The current source I1 is ideal → it carries no a.c. current, hence

           id1 + id2 = 0                            (3)

   Using (1) and (2) in (3):

           gm1 (vin – vs) – gm2 vs = 0
           ⇒ vs = gm1 /(gm1 + gm2) · vin            (4)

   Thus the follower gain is slightly less than unity; it becomes
   unity when gm1 ≫ gm2.

3. KCL at the output node  
   Ignoring ro2 for the moment (ro2 → ∞):

           id2 + vo/RD = 0
           –gm2 vs + vo/RD = 0
           ⇒ vo = gm2 RD · vs                       (5)

4. Overall voltage gain

           Av ≜ vo/vin
              = gm2 RD · gm1 /(gm1 + gm2)           (6)

   Special cases  
   • gm1 ≫ gm2 : Av ≈ gm2 RD          (almost an ideal common-gate)  
   • gm1 = gm2 : Av = (gm2 RD)/2  
   • gm2 ≫ gm1 : Av ≈ gm1 RD

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Including channel-length modulation (briefly)

If ro1 and ro2 are finite, substitute

   id1 = gm1 (vin – vs) + vs/ro1
   id2 = –gm2 vs + (vo – vs)/ro2

Carry the same two-node KCL procedure; the result is

   Av = (gm2 (RD || ro2)) · gm1 /[gm1 + gm2 + (RD || ro2)/ro1]

For ro1 , ro2 ≫ 1/gm the expression collapses to (6).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Important side results

Input resistance:
   Rin ≈ ∞      (gate of M1)

Small-signal resistance seen at node S:
   Rs ≈ 1/(gm1 + gm2)   (very low; good for driving the common-gate)

Output resistance:
   Rout ≈ RD || ro2

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Why use this topology?

1. A plain common-gate stage alone has a low input resistance (≈ 1/gm2); the added source follower raises the input resistance to a very large value without materially changing the gain.

2. The low impedance delivered by the follower to the source of M2
   pushes the pole at that node to a higher frequency, improving the
   bandwidth of the overall amplifier.

Hence the circuit provides
• high input impedance,
• gain ≈ gm2 RD,
• reasonably large output swing, and
• better high-frequency performance than a simple common-source stage with the same load.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as a source follower driving M2 as a common-gate stage, and gives the correct non-inverting gain. This satisfies the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
Step 1 – DC (large–signal) operating point  
Let  

 VS = source voltage of M1 and M2  
 ID1 = current of M1 (= current flowing from VDD through M1 into node S)  
 ID2 = current of M2 (= current flowing from RD through M2 into node S)

The ideal current sink forces

 I1 = ID1 + ID2                                        (1)

Assuming both devices operate in saturation,

 ID1 = ½ β1 (VIN – VS – VTH1)² (1+λ1VDS1)  
 ID2 = ½ β2 (VB – VS – VTH2)² (1+λ2VDS2)

(1) together with the two saturation inequalities

 VDD – VS ≥ VGS1         and  VOUT – VS ≥ VGS2

completely determines the bias point.  (In hand calculations one usually neglects λ and solves the quadratic equality for VS, then checks the two saturation conditions.)

Step 2 – Small–signal model  
• The current source I1 has infinite small–signal resistance → it is an open circuit.  
• M1 is a source follower (common-drain).  
• M2 is a common-gate stage (its gate is at the fixed, ac-grounded bias VB).  
• RD is the load resistor.

Small-signal equivalent:

 At node S (source of both transistors) we have  
  gm1(vin – vs)  + vs/ro1          (current through M1)  
 + (–gm2vs)       + (vs–vout)/ro2   (current through M2)  = 0        (2)

Step 3 – Source-follower gain (M1)  
Solve (2) for vs / vin:

 Av₁ ≡ vs / vin = gm1 ro1 / [1 + gm1ro1 + gm2ro2(1 + ro1/ro2)]   ≈ 1

(The approximation holds because gm1ro1 ≫ 1 and ro1 ≫ ro2 in most practical designs; in the ideal case ro1 → ∞, Av₁ → 1 exactly.)

Hence, to first order,

 vs ≈ vin.                                              (3)

Step 4 – Common-gate gain (M2)  
With the gate at ac ground the small-signal drain current of M2 is

 id2 = gm2 vs + (vout – vs)/ro2.

The voltage appearing across RD is –id2 RD, giving

 vout = –[gm2 RD || ro2] vs.                            (4)

Step 5 – Overall voltage gain  
Use (3) in (4):

 Av ≡ vout / vin = –gm2 (RD || ro2)         ≈  –gm2 RD     (if ro2 ≫ RD).     (5)

Thus the cascade behaves as a high-gain inverting amplifier whose magnitude is set almost completely by gm2 and RD; transistor M1 only level-shifts the input and contributes negligibly to the gain.

Step 6 – Input and output impedances  
Input resistance: RIN ≈ ∞ (MOS gate).  
Output resistance (seen looking into Vout with Vin = 0):

 Rout ≈ RD || [ro2(1 + gm2 rS)]  with  rS ≈ ro1 (∥ ∞)  
    ≈ gm2 ro2 RD    (if the tail current source is ideal and ro1 large).  

So Rout is substantially larger than RD alone, another consequence of the common-gate configuration.

Salient properties of the topology  
1. High gain with only one explicit resistor (RD).  
2. Very high input impedance.  
3. Minimal Miller effect at the input, hence wide bandwidth.  
4. Convenient biasing: the source follower places the M2 source at the proper dc level while presenting unity small-signal gain.

In short, Figure 20 is a “source-follower-driven common-gate” amplifier whose low-frequency gain is approximately –gm2 RD, input impedance is essentially infinite, and output impedance is high, making it attractive for wide-band, high-gain voltage amplification.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the source-follower-driven common-gate topology, but incorrectly treats M1 as an unloaded unity-gain follower and concludes the overall gain is inverting. The shared-source coupling gives a non-inverting gain; the erroneous sign limits the score to 3.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
The schematic is nothing more than a “source-follower-to-common-gate” cascade:

• M1 (left) is a source follower: gate = Vin , drain tied to the supply, source is the internal node S.  
• M2 (right) is a common-gate amplifier: gate is fixed at the dc bias Vb (an ac ground), source = S, drain = Vout, load = RD.  
• I1 is a tail current that biases both transistors; at dc the current splits so that I1 = ID1 + ID2.  
We analyse the bias conditions first and then the small-signal behaviour.

─────────────────────────────────────────
1.  DC (large–signal) conditions
─────────────────────────────────────────
Let VS be the voltage of the common source node.

• M1 (saturation)  ID1 = ½ kn1(W/L)1 (Vin – VS – VTH1)^2  
• M2 (saturation)  ID2 = ½ kn2(W/L)2 (Vb – VS – VTH2)^2  

with the constraint              ID1 + ID2 = I1

Together with the two “over-drive” equations the three unknowns VS , ID1 , ID2 can be found for a given Vin, Vb and I1.  In practice Vb is chosen so that both devices stay in saturation over the intended Vin range (e.g.  
VDD – VS ≥ VGS1 – VTH1  and  
Vout(min) ≥ Vb – VTH2).

─────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Small–signal model
─────────────────────────────────────────
(Neglect body effect for clarity, keep all gds.)

Node S  (source of both devices)  

( gds1 + gm1 + gds2 + gm2 ) vS  – gds2 vO  = gm1 vIN      …(1)

Node O  (drain of M2)  

( gm2 – gds2 ) vS  +  ( gds2 + gR ) vO  = 0                …(2)

where gR = 1/RD and  vO = vout , vIN = vin .

Solving (1) and (2) for Av = vO / vIN gives

        – gm1 gm2
Av  =  ------------------------------                      (3)
       (gm1+gm2+gds1+gds2)(gR+gds2) – gds2(gm2–gds2)

Useful limits

• gds1 , gds2  «  gm1 , gm2                   ⇒

        – gm1 gm2
   Av ≈ --------------  · 1/(gR)                                       (4)
        gm1 + gm2

• choose gm1  ≫  gm2 (normal sizing)          ⇒

   Av ≈ – gm2 RD                                             (5)

Equation (5) is the textbook result: the overall voltage gain is essentially that of the common-gate transistor (–gm2 RD); the source follower contributes a factor very nearly equal to 1 and therefore does not dilute the gain.

─────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Impedances
─────────────────────────────────────────
Input resistance: Gate of M1 ⇒ Rin ≈ ∞ (only small gate leakage and Cgs1).  

Output resistance (Vin = 0):

   Rout ≈ RD ∥ ro2 (1 + gm2 ro2)  ≃ RD          if gm2 ro2 ≫ 1

─────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Why this topology is attractive
─────────────────────────────────────────
1. High input impedance – the signal source only sees the gate of M1.  
2. Low-impedance node S (≈1/gm1) allows the common-gate device to be driven without the usual attenuation one gets when a high-impedance signal source is connected directly to the source of a CG stage.  
3. Large gain set almost entirely by gm2 and RD, independent of M1.  
4. Small input capacitance: the large gate capacitance of M2 is hidden behind the follower, so bandwidth is improved compared with a plain common-source stage having the same gain.  
5. One accurate bias current (I1) and one bias voltage (Vb) are all that is required to guarantee both devices stay in saturation.

─────────────────────────────────────────
Summary
─────────────────────────────────────────
Figure 20 realises a two-transistor gain cell in which a source follower (M1) with unity gain and high input resistance drives the low-impedance source of a common-gate amplifier (M2).  With usual sizing (gm1 ≫ gm2) the low-frequency gain is

        Av ≈ –gm2 RD ,

the input resistance is essentially infinite, and the dominant pole is at the output node (τ ≈ (RD ∥ ro2)·CLOAD), yielding a wide-band, single-pole, well-behaved amplifier stage.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as a source follower driving M2 as a common-gate stage and describes the shared bias current. However, it gives an inverting gain, whereas the signal path is non-inverting, and its unity-follower and gain conclusions are only conditional on gm1 being much larger than gm2.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
First look at the node at which we want to measure the small-signal output impedance, Vout.  
To obtain Zout we set the signal source Vin to ac ground, i.e. the left side of RS is at ground.  
With this condition the small-signal circuit that is relevant for Zout is

• the current-source transistor M2, whose ro is large and can be regarded as an open circuit,  
• the source follower transistor M1 with transconductance gm1, gate-source capacitance Cgs1 and drain-source conductance gds1 (ro1 = 1/gds1), and  
• the resistor RS that connects the gate of M1 to ground.

               Cgs1
      gate o─┤│├── RS ──► ac ground
             │ │
             │ │
             ▼ ▼
           +----+      id = gm1·vgs
 Vout o────┤ M1 ├─── ro1 ─► ac ground (VDD)
           +----+

1. Small-signal relations  
   Let the small-signal voltage applied at the output node be vS (= Vout) and the corresponding current that we have to supply be iS.  
   vG is the voltage that appears at the gate through RS.

   Gate equation (current through Cgs1):  
        iG = s Cgs1 (vG – vS)

   This gate current must flow through RS to ground, therefore  
        vG = –iG RS  = –s RS Cgs1 (vG – vS)

        ⇒ vG = [ s RS Cgs1 / (1 + s RS Cgs1) ] vS          (1)

   Transistor equation (controlled current that leaves the source):  
        iT = –gm1 (vG – vS)                                (2)  
        (negative sign because id flows from drain to source)

2. Current that leaves the source node  
   The total current that the outside world has to furnish is

        iS = iT + iG = –gm1 (vG – vS) + s Cgs1 (vG – vS)

        Using (1) and doing some algebra,

        iS = ( gm1 + s Cgs1 ) 
             [ s RS Cgs1 / (1 + s RS Cgs1) ] vS  –  gm1 vS          (3)

   For frequencies well below 1/(RS Cgs1) (so that |s RS Cgs1| ≪ 1) the factor
        s RS Cgs1 / (1 + s RS Cgs1)  ≈  s RS Cgs1

   Substituting this approximation in (3) we obtain

        iS ≈ (gm1 + s Cgs1) s RS Cgs1 vS  –  gm1 vS
           ≈ –gm1 vS  +  s² RS Cgs1² vS  +  s RS Cgs1² vS       (4)

   Because s² RS Cgs1² is a second-order (small) term, to first order we can write

        iS ≈ –gm1 vS  +  s RS Cgs1² vS

3. Output impedance  
        Zout(s) = vS / iS
                ≈ 1/[gm1 – s RS Cgs1²]
                ≈ 1/gm1  +  s ( RS Cgs1 / gm1 )               (5)

   The first term, 1/gm1, is a resistance.  
   The second term has the form sL with

        L = RS Cgs1 / gm1

   sL = jωL is the impedance of an inductor.  Hence the expression shows that the
   impedance seen looking into Vout has an inductive component even though no
   physical inductance exists in the circuit.

4. Physical interpretation (gyrator view)  
   • Cgs1 stores electric energy.  
   • The transconductance gm1 converts the gate-to-source voltage into a current at
     the source, i.e. it “gyrates” the capacitor.  
   • The series resistor RS ensures that a change of the source voltage first charges
     Cgs1 and only afterwards alters the gate voltage; the resulting current therefore
     leads the voltage by 90°, exactly what an inductor does.  
   • The combination RS – Cgs1 – gm1 works like a gyrator-C network and
     transforms the gate capacitance into an equivalent inductance L =
     RS Cgs1/gm1 that is seen at the source (and thus at Vout).

Therefore the output impedance of the circuit can appear inductive because the
gate-source capacitance of M1 is “reflected” into the source node through the
transconductance of M1 and the series resistor RS, producing the same voltage–current
phase relationship that a real inductor would exhibit.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the source-follower setup and the relevant RS–Cgs1–gm1 mechanism, but its current derivation is incorrect and it omits the key transition from about 1/gm1 to RS. It also misses the condition RS > 1/gm1 for inductive behavior, so it overgeneralizes the conclusion.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
Set Vin = 0 V while we look into the output node (the usual small-signal procedure for finding Zout).  
Under this condition the gate of M1 is connected to ground through RS, and the only linear elements that still couple the gate to the output node are

• the gate-source capacitance Cgs1  
• the controlled current source gm1 vgs of M1.

1. Relation between vg and vout  
A small test voltage vout applied to the source of M1 forces a displacement current through Cgs1.  
Kirchhoff at the gate node gives  

 (vg – 0)/RS  +  sCgs1 (vg – vout) = 0  

 ⇒ vg = sCgs1 RS vout / (1 + sCgs1 RS)

2. Drain (-source) current drawn by M1  

 iout = gm1 (vg – vout)  
    = gm1 [ sCgs1 RS vout /(1 + sCgs1 RS) – vout ]  
    = – gm1 vout /(1 + sCgs1 RS)

3. Small-signal output impedance  

 Zout(s) = vout / iout = (1 + sCgs1 RS)/gm1  
     = 1/gm1  +  s (RS Cgs1)/gm1.

The first term is a pure resistance (1/gm1).  
The second term is proportional to s = jω, exactly the form of the impedance of an inductor:

 Leq = RS Cgs1 / gm1.

As long as ω is well below the frequency at which other device parasitics become important (ω ≪ 1/RS Cgs1 and ω ≪ gm1/Cgs1), the imaginary part jω Leq dominates over any stray capacitance, so the node behaves like an inductor of value Leq in series with a small resistance 1/gm1.

Physically, RS and Cgs1 create a voltage at the gate that lags the source voltage; the transconductance of M1 converts this voltage difference into a current that is proportional to the time-derivative of vout – the hallmark of inductive behaviour.  The combination of the resistor, the gate-source capacitor and the transistor’s gm therefore realises a gyrator that “transforms” the capacitance into an equivalent inductance, making the output impedance of the circuit appear inductive.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the relevant RS–Cgs1 phase shift and gm mechanism, but omits the capacitor current at the output. Thus its impedance expression and inductance are incorrect: the actual high-frequency limit is RS, and inductive behavior requires RS > 1/gm.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
Set Vin to ac-ground (this is what we do when we measure Zout).  
Now the gate of the upper transistor M1 is connected to ground only through the
real resistor RS.

1.  Apply a small ac test voltage vout at the output node (the source of M1).

2.  Because of the gate-source capacitance Cgs (and the small Cgd),
    part of vout is coupled to the gate.  
    The gate current has nowhere to go except through RS, so the
    gate voltage is obtained from the simple RC equation

          vg + RS·Cgs·s (vg – vout) = 0     ⇒
          vg = (s RS Cgs) / (1 + s RS Cgs) · vout.

3.  The small-signal Vgs is therefore  

          vgs = vg – vout =
                – vout / (1 + s RS Cgs).

4.  The drain (source) current produced by M1 is

          id = gm · vgs ≈ – gm / (1 + s RS Cgs) · vout.

5.  Look at the frequency region in which  
          1/(RS Cgs)  ≪  ω  ≪  gm / Cgs.  
    In this band  |s RS Cgs| ≫ 1, so

          vgs ≈ – vout / (s RS Cgs)
          id  ≈ – gm /(s RS Cgs) · vout
               =  j ω (RS Cgs / gm) · vout.

6.  Therefore the small-signal impedance seen at the output node is

          Zout(ω) = vout / id ≈ j ω L, with L = RS Cgs / gm.

A positive imaginary impedance of the form j ω L is exactly what an
inductor exhibits.  
Hence the combination “RS + MOSFET (gm) + Cgs” behaves like a gyrator that
converts the transistor’s gate-source capacitance into an equivalent
inductance L = RS Cgs / gm, so over the stated frequency range the
output impedance is inductive even though no physical inductor is present.
(The lower transistor M2 merely provides the dc bias current; its ro is
large and does not affect this argument.)

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the Rs–Cgs feedback and an inductive band; the stated bounds imply gmRs is large. However, it incorrectly converts the current expression into a quantity proportional to jωRsCgs/gm, making the current and impedance steps inconsistent, and it does not explicitly show the low-to-high-frequency transition.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
Below is a systematic (dc-, small-signal- and qualitative) study of the “current-input, positive-feedback” stage of Fig. 22.

--------------------------------------------------
1.  Circuit description and signal flow
--------------------------------------------------
•  M1, RD1 and VDD form a common-source amplifier:
        VX (gate of M1)  →  ID1  →  vo (at the drain).

•  M2 conducts the input current Iin that is forced into node X;   
  its gate is driven by the output voltage vo, so

        vo (gate of M2)  →  ID2 (= Iin)  →  VX.

Hence a complete loop exists:

        vo  →  M2  →  VX  →  M1  →  vo

and the loop is **regenerative (positive feedback)**, as will be
evident from the algebra below.

Assumptions used in the analysis  
– Both transistors operate in saturation.  
– Body effect is ignored.  
– Long-channel device equations are used; λ is kept where
  necessary to expose the feedback that is hidden if ro = ∞.  
– µnCox is identical for the two devices.

Notation  
βk = µnCox (W/L)k         gm,k = ∂IDk/∂VGS        ro,k = 1/λkIDk

--------------------------------------------------
2.  Large-signal (dc) relations
--------------------------------------------------
Node X (KCL)

        Iin = ID2                                       (1)

ID2 = ½β2(VGS2)^2(1 + λ2VDS2)
      = ½β2( vo – VTH )^2 [1 + λ2VX]           (2)

Output node (KCL)

        ID1 = (VDD – vo)/RD1                    (3)

ID1 = ½β1(VX – VTH )^2 (1 + λ1vo)              (4)

Equations (1)…(4) give VX and vo for any Iin.  
If λ1 ≈ λ2 ≈ 0 the expressions simplify:

        VX ≈ VTH + √(2 Iin/β2)                (5)

        vo ≈ VDD – (β1/β2) Iin RD1            (6)

Equation (6) already shows that the stage is a **current-to-voltage converter (transimpedance amplifier)** whose gain is set by the ratio β1/β2 and by RD1.

--------------------------------------------------
3.  Small-signal (incremental) analysis
--------------------------------------------------
Let vx and vo denote the incremental voltages at X and at the
output; iin is the incremental input current.

Node X (KCL)

        iin = gm2 vo + (1/ro2)( vx – vo )      (7)

Output node (KCL)

        gm1 vx + vo( 1/RD1 + 1/ro1 ) = 0       (8)

From (8)

        vx = – vo ( 1/RD1 + 1/ro1 ) / gm1       (9)

Insert (9) into (7):

iin = gm2 vo – (1/ro2) vo[ 1 + (1/RD1 + 1/ro1)/gm1 ]   (10)

Hence the **small-signal transimpedance**

                vo / iin  ≡  RTI  =  1
                ───────────────────────────             (11)
                gm2 – (1/ro2) { 1 + (1/RD1 + 1/ro1)/gm1 }

Positive feedback term  
The second term in the denominator is subtracted from gm2; it
originates from the path vo → M2 → vx → M1 → vo.  
If

        gm2  ≈  (1/ro2) { 1 + (1/RD1 + 1/ro1)/gm1 }

the denominator tends to zero and |RTI| → ∞ : the circuit becomes
bistable (regenerates).  Stability therefore requires

        gm2 ro2  >  1 + (1/RD1 + 1/ro1)/gm1     (12)

In practice ro2 is finite but small, so the loop gain can be set
with transistor dimensions or by choosing RD1.

If ro1,ro2 → ∞ equation (11) collapses to

        RTI ≈ –1/gm2                           (13)

explaining why –even without high-gain op-amps– a useful,
reasonably accurate transimpedance (≈ –1/gm2) is obtained.

--------------------------------------------------
4.  Qualitative behaviour (why the loop is positive)
--------------------------------------------------
•  Suppose Iin increases slightly.  
•  This tries to raise vx (because M2 cannot instantly carry the
  extra current).  
•  Higher vx → M1 draws more current → vo falls.  
•  A lower vo reduces the gate voltage of M2, so M2 carries even
  **less** current, allowing vx to rise further.  
Each step reinforces the previous one – i.e. positive feedback.

--------------------------------------------------
5.  Key properties and design knobs
--------------------------------------------------
1.  Transimpedance magnitude  
        |RTI| ≈ (β1/β2) RD1     (λ ≈ 0 case)  
   It is increased by making M1 wider or M2 narrower, or by using a
   larger RD1.

2.  Input resistance  
        rin ≈ 1/gm2   (≲ a few hundred Ω), so the input node is
   nearly a **virtual ground for current signals**.

3.  Regeneration / latching  
   If the inequality (12) is intentionally violated the stage
   switches to one of two stable states; the topology is therefore
   widely used as the front end of sense amplifiers and current
   comparators.

--------------------------------------------------
6.  Summary
--------------------------------------------------
The circuit of Fig. 22 converts a current applied to node X into an
output voltage across RD1 while employing a regenerative path
(vo→M2→VX→M1→vo).  
•  For moderate loop gain it behaves as a transimpedance amplifier
  with gain ≈ –(β1/β2)RD1 and input resistance ≈ 1/gm2.  
•  As the product gm1 RD1 ro2 approaches gm2, the regeneration
  raises the gain sharply and eventually produces bistability.  
Tuning device sizes therefore allows the designer to move the
circuit smoothly from a linear TIA to a high-speed current
comparator/sense amplifier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies M2’s gate as tied to Vout, describes the positive-feedback loop through M1 and M2, and explicitly states bistability/latching as a consequence, satisfying the golden full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
The schematic of Fig-22 can be looked at as two elementary blocks that have been “chained” so that the output of one of them is taken back to the input of the other:

1.  M1, together with the load resistor RD1, is an ordinary common-source stage  
        vx  →  (-gm1 RD1)  →  vout

2.  M2 converts the output voltage of the first block back to a current that is drawn from node X:  
        vout  →  (gm2)  →  id2 = gm2 vout

Because the current of block-2 is applied to the same node that carries the original input current Iin, the loop is closed and the circuit exhibits positive (regenerative) feedback.

────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Large–signal (dc) operating point
────────────────────────────────────────
Assume both MOSFETs are in saturation.  
Id2 = Iin forced by the current source, hence

      Iin = ½ β2 (Vout − VT2)^2            (1)
      ⇒   Vout = VT2 + √(2 Iin/β2)         (1a)

The current through RD1 is Id1 = (VDD − Vout)/RD1.  
Since Id1 = ½ β1 (Vx − VT1)^2,

      Vx = VT1 + √(2(VDD − Vout)/(β1 RD1)) (2)

Equations (1a) and (2) completely define the dc solution.

────────────────────────────────────────
2.  Small–signal model
────────────────────────────────────────
For small variations (iin, vx, vout) about the bias point, neglect ro-effects and gate currents.

Output node (drain of M1):
      vout/RD1  +  gm1 vx  =  0
      ⇒ vout = –gm1 RD1 vx                     (3)

Input node X:
      iin − gm2 vout = 0
      ⇒ iin = gm2 vout                         (4)

Solve (3) and (4):

      vout =  iin / gm2                        (5)
      vx   = –iin /(gm1 gm2 RD1)               (6)

Important small-signal quantities

• Voltage gain of the common-source stage
      Av = vout/vx = –gm1 RD1

• Transimpedance (current → voltage)
      ZT = vout/iin = 1/gm2        (purely resistive)

• Small-signal input resistance seen at node X
      Rin = vx/iin = –1/(gm1 gm2 RD1) (negative!)

────────────────────────────────────────
3.  Nature of the feedback
────────────────────────────────────────
The loop gain is

      T = (-gm1 RD1)·(gm2) = –gm1 gm2 RD1

Its sign is negative, which means that the feedback returned to node X is in phase with the original disturbance; i.e. the feedback is positive (regenerative).

A useful way to see it qualitatively:  
• Let vout rise slightly.  
• gm2 vout therefore grows, pulling more current from node X.  
• vx falls, so M1 conducts less drain current.  
• The drop in ID1 lets Vout rise still further.  
The disturbance is reinforced – the hallmark of positive feedback.

────────────────────────────────────────
4.  Implications and practical use
────────────────────────────────────────
1.  Because Rin is negative, the circuit can be used as a “negative-resistance” element for oscillators or impedance-cancellation networks.

2.  |T| = gm1 gm2 RD1 determines how strong the regeneration is.  
   • |T| < 1  → the circuit behaves linearly with finite negative Rin.  
   • |T| ≥ 1  → the loop can break into bistability or oscillation, depending on the parasitics that were ignored in the ideal analysis.

3.  The transimpedance is set almost entirely by gm2; by choosing W/L of M2 one can design a precise current-to-voltage converter whose output is largely independent of gm1 and RD1, provided the loop stays in the linear region.

Thus the circuit of Fig-22 is a compact current-input stage that employs positive feedback to obtain a high voltage gain, a controllable transimpedance of 1/gm2, and a (generally unwanted but sometimes very useful) negative input resistance of –1/(gm1 gm2 RD1).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes that M2 is controlled by Vout, identifies the regenerative M1–M2 feedback loop, and states negative input resistance and possible bistability, meeting the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
Explanation of the topology (what is connected to what)

1.  M1 : n-MOS used as a common–source amplifier.  
    – Drain : node Vout  
    – Gate  : node X  
    – Source: ground  
    – Load  : RD1 that returns to VDD

2.  M2 : n-MOS whose  
    – Drain : node X (same node that drives the gate of M1)  
    – Gate  : node Vout (the output of the first stage)  
    – Source: ground

3.  Iin : a dc (or slowly varying) current injected into node X.

Hence the signal path is

      X  →  M1+RD1  →  Vout  →  M2  →  X

so whatever leaves node X through M2 is determined by the present value of
Vout, and Vout itself is determined by the present value of X.  
This closes a loop around the two transistors.

-------------------------------------------------------------
1.  Large–signal (d.c.) relations
-------------------------------------------------------------

For hand analysis assume both devices operate in strong inversion,
λ  ≈  0 (to keep the algebra short), and use the square-law model.

M1 in saturation
        ID1 = (k1/2) (VX – VT)²                         (1)

The output node is loaded by RD1 :

        Vout = VDD – ID1 RD1                            (2)

M2 usually remains in the triode region because VDS2 = VX is small
while VGS2 = Vout can be close to VDD.  
With VDS2 ≤ VGS2 – VT we may write

        ID2 = k2 [ (Vout – VT) VX – ½ VX² ]            (3)

The only d.c. current leaving node X is the current of M2, therefore

        Iin = ID2                                       (4)

Equations (2) and (4) give two curves in the (VX , Vout) plane:  
– (2) is a downward–opening parabola.  
– (4) is a straight, almost vertical line because ID2 depends mainly
  on Vout through its gate.

Depending on the value of Iin the two curves intersect in either  
• one point (no regeneration) or  
• three points (two stable + one unstable ⇒ latch / hysteresis).

-------------------------------------------------------------
2.  Small–signal loop-gain
-------------------------------------------------------------

Take small variations around an operating point and define

        gm1 = ∂ID1/∂VX         (transconductance of M1)
        gm2 = ∂ID2/∂Vout       (transconductance of M2’s gate)  
        gd2 = ∂ID2/∂VX         (drain conductance of M2)

Step–by–step:

ΔVX   →   ΔID1 = gm1 ΔVX

through RD1 (with a – sign because the transistor pulls current
downwards):

ΔVout = – gm1 RD1 ΔVX                              (5)

A change of Vout alters the current of M2:

ΔID2 =  + gm2 ΔVout  – gd2 ΔVX                    (6)

Node-X carries no small-signal source (ΔIin = 0 in loop analysis),
so the incremental currents must cancel:

          gm2 ΔVout – gd2 ΔVX = 0                 (7)

Substitute (5) in (7):

          gm2 (– gm1 RD1 ΔVX) – gd2 ΔVX = 0

       ΔVX [ gm1 gm2 RD1 / gd2  – 1 ] = 0

Hence the closed-loop (regenerative) gain is

          T = gm1 gm2 RD1 / gd2                   (8)

•  If T < 1  →  the loop is stable and behaves like an ordinary
   current-to-voltage amplifier.  
•  If T > 1  →  two of the loop poles move to the right-half plane,
   the intermediate operating point becomes unstable and the circuit
   snaps to one of the two extreme solutions (regeneration).

-------------------------------------------------------------
3.  Trip points (current hysteresis)
-------------------------------------------------------------

HIGH-state (Vout ≈ VDD)   
M1 is OFF (VX < VT) so ID1 ≈ 0, Vout ≈ VDD.  
The current that keeps the node in this state is the current that M2
can sink when VX is just below threshold (VX ≈ VT-).  

        IH ≈ k2 [ (VDD – VT) VT – ½ VT² ]           (9)

LOW-state (Vout ≈ 0)  
With Vout ≈ 0 the gate of M2 is at 0 V and M2 is OFF; all of Iin must
be sunk by M1.  The state disappears when VX falls to VT:

        IL ≈ 0  (ideal square-law, more precisely a few µA in practice)

Therefore the circuit behaves like a **current-input Schmitt trigger**:
for IL < Iin < IH the output keeps its previous value; crossing IH
sends Vout “LOW”, crossing IL sends it “HIGH”.

-------------------------------------------------------------
4.  Design guide-lines
-------------------------------------------------------------

•  Increase gm1 (wider M1), increase RD1 or make M2 long (small gd2)
   to make T larger and obtain crisper regeneration.

•  Decrease gm2 (narrower M2) if only a modest gain without
   bistability is desired.

-------------------------------------------------------------
5.  What the circuit is good for
-------------------------------------------------------------

Because it converts a small d.c. or slowly-varying **current** into a
full rail-to-rail **voltage** while consuming only two MOSFETs and one
resistor, the cell of Fig. 22 is found in

• Ultra-low-power current comparators  
• Photo-detector front ends (Iin supplied by a photodiode)  
• Sense-amplifiers and data-latches in low-supply memories  
• Relaxation oscillators (by adding a capacitor at node X)

In short: M1 + RD1 provide a high-gain inverting stage, M2 feeds the
output back with the same polarity, and the overall loop-gain
gm1 gm2 RD1 / gd2 decides whether the circuit acts as a linear
transimpedance amplifier or as a regenerative latch with hysteresis.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M2’s gate at Vout, the positive-feedback loop, and the resulting instability/latching when loop gain exceeds one, satisfying the full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
Figure 23 implements a shunt-shunt (current-to-voltage) feedback amplifier, i.e. a trans-impedance amplifier (TIA).  
The two MOS/resistor stages furnish a large open–loop gain and the feedback resistor RF then fixes the closed-loop transfer almost exclusively.  
Small-signal symbols:

gm1 , gm2  transconductances of M1, M2  
ro1 , ro2  output resistances (ignored for first-order work)  
RD1 , RD2 load resistors  
RF    feedback resistor  
vs , vx , vout small-signal voltages at the source of M1, the drain of M1, and the output node, respectively.  
iin    input current to be converted to a voltage.

1. Open-loop gain (RF removed)  
– M1 is used in common-gate mode; its small-signal input resistance is Rin0 ≈ 1/gm1.  
   id1 = –gm1 vs                (1)  
   vx  = –gm1 RD1 vs           (2)  
– M2 is a common-source stage:  
   vout = –gm2 RD2 vx          (3)  
Combining (2) and (3) gives  
   vout = (gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2) vs  ≡ A0 vs             (4)  
Hence the open-loop voltage gain is  

 A0 ≅ gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2                              (5)

(With the polarities shown this gain is positive; if the directions are reversed one sign changes.)

2. Adding the feedback network  
Current through RF (arrow in the figure):  
   iRF = (vs – vout)/RF                             (6)

KCL at the input node (currents entering the node positive):  

   iin – gm1 vs – iRF = 0                           (7)

Insert (6) and (4) into (7) and solve for vout/iin:

   iin – gm1 vs – (vs – vout)/RF = 0  
   ⇒ iin = gm1 vs + (vs – A0 vs)/RF  
   ⇒ vs = iin /[gm1 + (A0–1)/RF]                    (8)  
   ⇒ vout = A0 vs = A0 iin /[gm1 + (A0–1)/RF]       (9)

The closed-loop trans-impedance is therefore  

 ZT ≡ vout / iin = A0 /[gm1 + (A0–1)/RF]            (10)

If A0 ≫ 1 and gm1 RF ≫ 1, (10) reduces to the familiar TIA result  

 ZT ≅ RF                                            (11)

Hence the feedback resistor alone determines the conversion accuracy, provided the amplifier gain is high enough.

3. Input impedance  
Rin = vs / iin = 1/[gm1 + (A0–1)/RF] ≈ RF/A0 ≈ 1/gm1 (very small) (12)

A very low Rin forces the photo- or sensor diode to sit at an (almost) ac ground, minimising the effect of its capacitance and greatly extending the bandwidth.

4. Loop-gain point of view  
Feedback factor β ≈ 1/RF, so the loop gain is  

 T = A0 β ≈ A0 /RF                                  (13)

Large |T| provides the precision of (11) but must be limited for stability; the dominant pole is usually placed at Vout (RD2 ‖ CL), the non-dominant at node X.

5. Summary of important properties

• Closed-loop trans-impedance ZT ≈ RF  
• Input resistance      Rin ≈ 1/gm1 ≪ RF  
• Output resistance     Rout ≈ RD2 (slightly lowered by feedback)  
• Bandwidth (first order)     f–3 dB ≈ 1/(2π Rin CPD) (CPD = diode capacitance)  
• Accuracy condition    gm1 RF ≫ 1 and A0 ≫ 1.

Thus the circuit of Fig. 23 is a two-stage, high-gain amplifier closed with a shunt resistor so that:

 Input current → almost entirely through RF → output voltage ≈ Iin · RF,

while at the same time presenting the current source with an exceptionally low-impedance (virtual-ground) node.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, M2 as a common-source stage driven by X, and RF as the feedback path forming a TIA. But its positive open-loop gain and +RF transfer imply the wrong feedback polarity; its KCL algebra also reverses the sign of 1−A0. The circuit has negative feedback and a −RF high-loop-gain transimpedance, so the explicit cap for positive-feedback reasoning applies.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
Circuit of Fig. 23 in one sentence  
A two–stage, resistively-loaded CMOS amplifier (M1 common-gate, M2 common-source) is closed around the resistor RF, so that the input current Iin is converted to a voltage –Iin RF with very low error; the active devices merely supply the large loop gain that forces the “virtual-ground” behaviour at the input node.

Step-by-step small-signal analysis

1.  Label the small-signal variables  
    vS : voltage of the summing node (source of M1, one side of RF)  
    vX : drain of M1 / gate of M2  
    vout : amplifier output

2.  Small-signal models  
    • M1 (common-gate) : gm1, ro1, input resistance Rin,ol ≈ 1/gm1  
    • M2 (common-source) : gm2, ro2  
    • RD1 , RD2 : linear loads, RF : feedback element

3.  Open-loop transimpedance  (RF open-circuited)  
    Ignoring ro-effects for clarity:

        vX  =  (-iS) RD1                 (drain current of M1 flows through RD1)
        vout=  (-gm2 RD2) vX
              =  –gm2 RD2 RD1 iS

        Zol ≡ vout / iS  ≈  –gm2 RD2 RD1        …(1)

4.  Input resistance of the bare amplifier  
        Rin,ol ≡ vS / iS ≈ 1 / gm1              …(2)

   (tens of ohms for a few-mA/V gm1)

5.  Close the loop with RF  
   KCL at the summing node:

        iin + iRF + (-iS) = 0
        iRF = (vout – vS)/RF

   Eliminate iS with (1) and vS with (2):  

        vout = Zol (iin + (vout – vS)/RF)  
        vS   = Rin,ol (iin + (vout – vS)/RF)

   Solve for the closed-loop transimpedance:

        Zt ≡ vout / iin =  – RF · 1 / [ 1 + T ]        …(3)

        T = |loop-gain| ≈ (gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2) / RF       …(4)

   Because |T| ≫ 1 in a properly designed circuit,  

        vout ≈ – iin RF                                …(5)

   so the gain is set almost entirely by the resistor RF.

6.  Properties with feedback  

    • Input (photodiode) impedance  

          Zin = vS / iin ≈ Rin,ol /(1+T) ≈ RF /(gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2)

      Typically a few milliohms – the node behaves as a virtual ground.  

    • Sensitivity of the gain to device parameters ≈ 1/T (very small).  

    • Output swing limited by saturation of M1 and M2:  
          Vheadroom ≈ Vov1 + Vov2 ;  |iin|max ≈ (VDD – Vheadroom)/RF.

7.  Bandwidth (dominant pole at node X)  

        ωp,ol ≈ 1 / [ (RD1 || ro1) · CX ]  
        f-3dB,cl ≈ |T| · f-p,ol                (feedback widens the BW)

8.  Noise (referred to input current)  

        i^2n,total ≈ 4kT/RF  +  (4/3) γ kT gm1  +  …  
        Increasing RF raises both gain and resistor noise; gm1 sets the
        second term.

Key numerical relations to remember

    Open-loop: Zol ≈ –gm2 RD2 RD1
               Rin,ol ≈ 1/gm1

    Loop-gain: |T| ≈ gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2 / RF

    Closed-loop:  Vout ≈ – Iin RF
                  Zin  ≈ RF / (gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2)

Thus the circuit is a classical CMOS transimpedance amplifier whose accuracy is defined by RF, while M1–M2 provide the large, but otherwise uncritical, gain needed to enforce it.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, X as driving the common-source M2 stage, and RF as feedback from Vout to the input node, forming a transimpedance amplifier. This meets the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
Circuit operation  
1.  Bias conditions  
   •  M1 and M2 are biased in saturation with a dc gate voltage Vb that
      makes the quiescent drain current of M1 roughly  
         ID ≈ (Vb – Vth1)²k/2,  
      so that node X sits somewhere near the middle of the supply and
      both transistors have adequate VDS for signal swing.  
   •  RD1 and RD2 carry this bias current and establish the dc voltages
      at X and Vout.

2.  Small-signal model  
   •  Let vS be the small signal at the source of M1 (the “input node’’),
      vX at node X and vout at the drain of M2.  
   •  With the gate of M1 tied to the ac ground (Vb is fixed) the small
     -signal drain current of M1 is ­gm1 vS (negative because the signal
      is applied to the source).  
   •  M1 therefore behaves like a common-source amplifier whose gain is  
         Av1 = vX / vS ≈ –gm1 (RD1 ∥ ro1).  
   •  M2 is an ordinary common-source stage:  
         Av2 = vout / vX ≈ –gm2 (RD2 ∥ ro2).  
   •  Open-loop voltage gain of the two-stage amplifier  
         Av ≡ vout / vS ≈ gm1 gm2 (RD1 ∥ ro1)(RD2 ∥ ro2)
         (two minus signs → overall positive gain).

3.  Closing the loop with RF (trans-impedance mode)  
   •  KCL at the input node (source of M1):

         Iin = is + (vS – vout)/RF          with  is = –gm1 vS

         ⇒ Iin = –gm1 vS + (vS – vout)/RF
                = –gm1 vS + (1 – Av) vS / RF          (because vout = Av vS)

   •  Solve for the closed-loop transfer function (trans-impedance)

         ZT ≡ vout / Iin
            = Av vS / Iin
            = Av / [ –gm1 + (1 – Av)/RF ]
            = –RF Av / (Av – gm1 RF – 1)

   •  If   Av ≫ (gm1 RF + 1)   the denominator ≈ Av and

         ZT ≈ –RF

     so the circuit acts as an inverting current-to-voltage converter:
         vout ≈ – Iin RF.

   •  Input node voltage (the “virtual ground’’)

         vS = Iin /[ –gm1 + (1 – Av)/RF ]  ≈ – Iin RF / Av

     is very small, therefore the input impedance

         Rin = vS / Iin ≈ RF / Av  ≪ 1/gm1,

     insuring that virtually the whole sensor current flows through RF.

4.  Poles and stability  
   •  First pole at node X:  ωp1 ≈ 1 / [ (RD1 ∥ ro1) CX ],  
      where CX is the total capacitance at X.  
   •  Second pole at the output:  ωp2 ≈ 1 / [ (RD2 ∥ ro2 ∥ RF) CL ].  
   •  To keep the loop stable make the 0-dB frequency (≈ 1/RF · |ZT|) well
      below ωp1, add Miller or lead compensation if necessary, or lower
      the resistive loads.

5.  Noise (dominant terms, referred to the input)  
      i²n,RF = 4kT / RF         (feedback resistor)  
      i²n,M1 = 4kT γ gm1        (channel noise of M1)  
      Other contributors (RD1, RD2, M2, etc.) are usually smaller once
      referred back by Av.

6.  Output swing limits  
      Vout,max ≈ VDD – (ID RD2 + VDSsat2)  
      Vout,min ≈ VDSsat2.  
      Node-X constraint:  vX ≥ vS + VDSsat1 to keep M1 saturated.

Summary  
•  M1 and M2 provide a large positive open-loop voltage gain  
     Av ≈ gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2.  
•  The feedback resistor RF forces the circuit to behave as a
  trans-impedance amplifier.  
•  For Av » 1 the ideal result is obtained:  
     vout = – Iin RF,  
  with very low input impedance and therefore excellent current sensing
  accuracy.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It places the input at M1’s source, identifies M2 as driven by X, and recognizes RF feedback with an approximate −RF transimpedance. However, it calls M1 common-source and uses the wrong gain sign, making its feedback and input-node derivation inconsistent with the actual common-gate topology.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
(The terminals of the two MOSFET symbols are drawn in the usual way for a p–channel device: the upper terminal is the source, the lower one the drain and the gate is the vertical plate that touches neither of them.  
All n-well/bulk terminals are tied to the highest supply, VDD.  
λ is taken different from zero only when the effect is explicitly mentioned, body effect is ignored.)

1.   DC operating point  

     a)  Currents  
         I1 is a (nearly) ideal current sink that fixes the dc drain current of M1.  
         IREF (the downward current source connected to the input node) fixes, together with
         Iin (which may be positive, negative or zero), the dc current that must be supplied to
         the input node by M2:  

                      I2  =  IREF  –  Iin                                    (1)

         With both transistors in saturation we therefore have  

                 I1 = ID1 = k1 (VSG1 – |VTP|)^2             (2)  
                 I2 = ID2 = k2 (VSG2 – |VTP|)^2             (3)

         where  k = ½μpCox(W/L).

     b)  Node voltages  

         From (2) Vout = Vb – |VTP| + √(I1/k1)             (4)

         From (3) Vx   = VDD – |VTP| – √(I2/k2)            (5)

         ΔIin therefore shows up only as a small change of Vx given by (5); Vout is determined
         almost exclusively by the bias quantities I1 and Vb.

2.   Small-signal behaviour  

     Small-signal quantities are written lower-case (vx , vout , iin …).

     •   Node X (input node)  

         KCL (the bias current sources are ideal, their incremental admittance is zero)

             id2 = –(gm2+gds2) vx                        (8)

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
Circuit operation (qualitative)  
•  M2 is a diode-connected PMOS.  Its large small-signal transconductance gm2 forces the common node x to sit at an almost fixed voltage  
  Vx ≃ VDD – |VTp| – |Vov2|.  
   Because rπ2 = 1/gm2 is small, node x behaves like a “virtual ground” for a-c signals.  

•  M1 is an NMOS operated in common–gate configuration; its drain is the output node.  
   The d.c. current I1 that is pulled out of Vout must flow through M1, so Id1 = I1 in quiescent condition.  

•  Iin is the signal current injected into node x.  Any change of Iin produces only a very small change of Vx; this change is sensed by M1, which converts it into a much larger change of its drain current.  Since I1 is fixed, the surplus or deficit of current charges the capacitance at Vout, producing the output-voltage swing.  The loop consisting of M1 and the low-impedance node x therefore realises negative feedback that converts input current into output voltage.

Small-signal analysis  
Let the small-signal variations be denoted by lower-case symbols (vx, vout, iin, id1).

1.  Input (node x) impedance  
  vx  =  iin / gm2   ⇒ Rin  =  vx / iin  ≈ 1/gm2 (usually only a few Ω).

2.  Current conversion  
  id1 = –gm1 · vx           (because vgs1 = –vx, the gate of M1 being at the fixed bias Vb).  
  ∴  id1 / iin = –gm1/gm2.

3.  Output voltage  
  The incremental resistance seen looking into the drain of M1 is ro1; the ideal current source I1 contributes roI1, so  
  Rout = ro1 ∥ roI1  (normally ≫ Rin).  
  vout = –id1 · Rout  
     =  (gm1/gm2) · Rout · iin.  

Hence the transimpedance (gain from input current to output voltage) is  

  Zt = vout / iin = (gm1 / gm2) · Rout. (positive polarity)

By sizing the two MOSFETs the ratio gm1/gm2 — and therefore the gain — can be set with good accuracy because it depends mainly on the W/L ratios, not on absolute device parameters.

Large-signal limits for correct saturation  
•  M2 saturated: VDD – Vx ≥ |VTp| + |Vov2|  
•  M1 saturated: Vout – Vx ≥ Vov1  
•  Current source head-room:  Vout ≤ VDD – VDSsat(I1)

These relations determine the maximum positive and negative values of Iin that can be accommodated without driving any device out of saturation.

Summary  
The network therefore realises a low-impedance current input (≈1/gm2), a controllable current gain of –gm1/gm2, and a high-impedance voltage output whose excursion equals the input current multiplied by (gm1/gm2)·Rout.  It is a simple one-transistor, ratio-controlled, current-to-voltage converter that uses the diode-connected PMOS as the feedback element that keeps the input node at (almost) a.c. ground.

This topology error leads to incorrect input resistance, output resistance, and transimpedance conclusions, so the central analysis is wrong.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
Circuit of Fig-24 in words  
• M2 is a diode-connected p-MOS that ties the node VX (the common point of M1-source and the two external current sources) to VDD through a low incremental resistance 1/gm2.  
• M1 is an n-MOS biased with a fixed gate voltage Vb; its drain is the output node and it is loaded by the ideal current source I1.  
• Iin represents the signal current that has to be converted into a voltage; the second dc current source that points downward only supplies the bias current that keeps the node alive when Iin = 0 (it can be merged with Iin in the equations).

I.  Large-signal (dc) operating point  
At node VX

 IM2 = IBIAS – Iin                       (1)

where IBIAS is the constant current delivered by the lower current source.  
Because M2 is diode-connected and assumed to be in saturation,

 IM2 = (k′p/2)(W/L)2 (VDD – VX – |VTp|)^2             (2)

so

 VX = VDD – |VTp| – √{2(IM2)/(k′pW/L)2}.              (3)

If device 2 is made wide, gm2 is large and √{…} varies only slightly with IM2; hence VX is almost constant for any reasonable excursion of Iin.  
With VX nearly fixed, the gate-source voltage of M1,

 VGS1 = Vb – VX                          (4)

also stays practically constant, so M1 remains in saturation and its dc drain current is almost independent of Iin. The output node voltage is fixed by

 ID1 = I1.                               (5)

II.  Small-signal analysis  
(λ-effects neglected for clarity; ro-values are inserted later.)

1.  Input (shunt) node VX  
For small signals let vx be the incremental voltage and iin the incremental input current.  
Diode-connected M2: id2 = gm2 · vx  
Source of M1 (gate fixed): id1 = –gm1 · vx (the sign is negative because an increase of vx decreases VGS1)  

KCL at VX gives  
 iin + (–gm1 vx) + (–gm2 vx) = 0 →  vx = iin /(gm1 + gm2)                (6)

Therefore

 Rin ≜ vx / iin = 1 /(gm1 + gm2) ≈ 1/gm2            (7)

(The input node behaves almost as a virtual ground; Rin can easily be < 100 Ω.)

2.  Output node Vout  
With an ideal current source I1 (infinite output resistance) the only small-signal current leaving node Vout is the incremental drain current of M1:

 gm1 (–vx) + vout/ro1 = 0 →  vout = –gm1 ro1 vx.                  (8)

Combining (6) and (8):

 vout / iin = – gm1 ro1 /(gm1 + gm2) ≈ –(gm1/gm2) ro1.              (9)

So the stage is a current-to-voltage converter (a trans-impedance amplifier) whose trans-resistance is set by the product ro1 and by the ratio gm1/gm2, while keeping a very small input impedance.

III.  Salient properties  
• Low input impedance: Rin ≈ 1/gm2 (tens of Ω with a few hundred µA and a wide device).  
• Large voltage gain: ro1 can be hundreds of kΩ, so a few-µA change in Iin yields several hundred millivolts at Vout.  
• Negative sign (inversion): a positive ΔIin raises VX, decreases ID1 and therefore lets Vout rise (because I1 is fixed).  
• Bandwidth: because the low Rin also kills the capacitance of node VX (cx ≈ Cin /gm2), the circuit is fast and is frequently called a “regulated cascode” or “active-feedback” input stage.  
• Saturation limits: to keep M1 in saturation Vout ≥ Vb – VTn; to keep M2 saturated VX ≤ VDD – |VTp|.

IV.  Typical design numbers (0.18-µm CMOS)  
gm1 ≈ 1 mS, gm2 ≈ 10 mS, ro1 ≈ 100 kΩ →  
Rin ≈ 100 Ω, Trans-impedance ≈ –10 kΩ, BW limited only by the capacitance tied to Vout.

In summary, the circuit realises a low-impedance current input node through the shunt feedback provided by the diode-connected PMOS (M2). Only a small fraction (gm1/gm2) of the input current is forced through M1; that small current flows into a high-resistance output node, producing a large voltage swing.

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 5 fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No – making the three load capacitors very large only slows the ring oscillator down; it does not eliminate the oscillation as long as the capacitances are still finite.

Why it keeps oscillating

1. Odd inversion: With three inverters the loop has an odd number of signal inversions, so a dc (steady-state) operating point is impossible unless every node sits exactly at the in-between (metastable) switching voltage. Any small perturbation from that metastable point drives the outputs toward one rail or the other, so the circuit must keep changing state.

2. Barkhausen criteria:  
   • Phase-shift requirement is always met (180° from the odd number of inverters → 360° total around the loop).  
   • Gain requirement is easiest to satisfy at low frequency because the small-signal gain of a CMOS inverter is maximum at dc.  
   If CL is increased, the dominant pole of each stage moves to a lower frequency, so the frequency at which the loop phase goes to 0° (mod 360°) moves down as well; the required loop gain at that lower frequency is actually larger, not smaller.

3. Charge-time argument: To flip one node, a charge Q = CL · VDD has to be sourced or sunk. With a finite drive current ID the time needed is t = Q / ID = CL · VDD / ID. If CL → ∞, t → ∞, so the oscillation frequency f = 1/(2·3·t) → 0, but for any finite CL the edge will eventually propagate and the ring will switch again.

Only two practical limits can stop it

• CL literally infinite.  
• CL so large that leakage currents equal the on-current of the transistors, preventing the node from ever reaching a logic threshold; in real silicon this occurs at some very large but finite value, not at any “ordinary” capacitance you can connect in a lab.

Therefore, in an ideal circuit the oscillator never “fails” – its period just becomes arbitrarily long as the capacitors become arbitrarily large.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that finite, larger capacitors slow the ring without stopping oscillation, and gives a valid charge-time argument. However, it incorrectly claims the required loop gain grows as capacitance increases, so it does not receive full credit.

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 5 fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No – making the three capacitors bigger does not prevent the ring oscillator from working; it only makes it slower.

Why it keeps oscillating  
1. Barkhausen criterion.  With three inverters the loop furnishes a fixed 180 ° phase shift.  
   Each inverter-plus-capacitor stage can be written (for small signals) as  

        A(s) = −K / (1 + sτ)         with  τ = Rdrive · CL.  

   At very low frequency (s → 0)  |A| = K , so the low-frequency loop-gain magnitude is |−K|^3 = K³.  
   For a normal CMOS inverter K (the small-signal gain at the switching point) is ≫1, so the
   magnitude is still >1 no matter how large CL is.  
   Therefore the magnitude will inevitably cross unity at some finite ω where the
   accumulated phase is still –180 °, so the Barkhausen conditions are satisfied and an
   oscillation exists.

2. Effect of a larger CL.  A larger CL increases τ, pushing the unity-gain frequency down:

        ωosc ≈ c / τ  ∝ 1/CL         →   Tosc ∝ CL.

   As CL → ∞ the period tends to ∞ and the frequency tends to 0, but for any finite CL the
   period is merely very long, not infinite.

3. Practical limit.  The circuit would only “fail” if the capacitors were literally infinite so
   the nodes could never move, or if the inverters could not supply the charge needed to
   change the voltage far enough to reach the switching threshold.  For any realizable,
   however large, capacitance the outputs will eventually charge/discharge through the
   finite on-resistance of the transistors and the loop will still regenerate.

So the ring oscillator does not stop oscillating when the three capacitors are made very large; its oscillation frequency just becomes correspondingly very low.

However, the Barkhausen explanation is flawed: low-frequency loop gain above unity does not ensure unity gain at the required phase condition. The correct phase condition is unchanged by scaling all three capacitors.

For any finite load capacitance each inverter can still charge- and discharge- that
capacitance, which merely increases the propagation delay of the stage

  τd ≈ Ro CL               (Ro = output resistance of the inverter).

The oscillation frequency of a three-stage ring is roughly

finite frequency always exists as long as CL is finite.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in Figure 5 are doubled?

answer.text:
To first order it does not change.

• Doubling every C​L makes the delay of each inverter ~2 × larger, so the oscillation frequency is cut in half.  
• The thermal-noise voltage that appears on a node goes down ( kT/C → ½ ), so σv ↓ √2.  
• At the same time the node is charged / discharged twice as slowly, so the slope at the switching instant (dV/dt) is also ↓ 2.  
• Time-jitter per edge is σt = σv /(dV/dt) ∝ (1/√C)/(1/C) = √C → it increases by 2, but the period T has also doubled, so the fractional timing error σt /T – and therefore the phase (jitter) variance – remains the same.  

Hence the single-sideband phase-noise density (dBc/Hz) is essentially unchanged; the only noticeable effect is that the carrier frequency has been reduced by a factor of two.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in Figure 5 are doubled?

answer.text:
In a ring oscillator the instantaneous phase error that a noise voltage vn produces is  

Δφ = (2π/T)·(vn /(dV/dt)) , with dV/dt ≈ I /CL   

(I is the average charging/discharging current of the inverter).  
The rms noise voltage at the output of an inverter is about vn,rms ≈ √(kT/CL).  
Hence the rms phase fluctuation is  

σφ ≈ 2π · √(kT/CL) · CL / (T·I)  
  = 2π · √(kT) / (I√CL) · (CL /T).  

Because the oscillation period itself is proportional to the load capacitance,  
T ≈ K·CL /I  (K is a constant that depends on the number of stages), we obtain  

σφ ∝ 1 /√CL .  

Therefore

• If every load capacitor is doubled (CL → 2CL),  
 σφ → σφ /√2  →  the phase-noise power (proportional to σφ²) is halved.  

Expressed in dB, the single-side-band phase-noise density improves by about  

10·log10(½) ≈ –3 dB.

So doubling the three capacitors lowers (improves) the phase noise by roughly 3 dB.

 td,new = 2·td,old ⇒ fosc,new = ½·fosc,old.

1. Time-jitter  
   The random voltage noise of the transistors produces the same rms timing uncertainty at the switching threshold, because  
   Δt ≈ ΔV /(dV/dt)   and both ΔV (∝1/C) and dV/dt (∝1/C) scale in the same way; hence σt is almost unchanged.

2. Converting time-jitter to phase-jitter  
   σφ = 2π fosc σt.

3. Phase-noise power

answers.question: Does the circuit in Figure 6 fail to oscillate if CL becomes arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
Not as long as the capacitor is still finite.  
A three-inverter ring has no dc logic solution (“1,0,1 …” cannot satisfy an odd number of inversions), so with any finite parasitic or explicit capacitance the only point the loop can sit at is the metastable point where every node is close to VDD /2.  
At that operating point the small-signal gain of each inverter is large (|A0| ≫ 1), so the loop gain |A0|^3 is also ≫ 1 and the metastable state is unstable: the slightest noise or mismatch forces one node to move, that movement propagates around the loop and an oscillation is created.

Putting an extra load CL on one of the nodes simply lowers the dominant pole of the first stage:

ωp = 1 /(Rdrive CL)

Hence the oscillation frequency

fosc ≈ 1 /(2 N Rdrive CL)  (N = 3 here)

is reduced roughly in proportion to CL.  
If CL is made larger and larger the period grows correspondingly, but as long as CL is finite the node can still be charged and discharged (dV/dt = I /CL) and the ring will eventually leave the metastable point and oscillate—just very slowly.

Only in the mathematical limit CL → ∞ (or in practice a value so large that the output devices can never supply enough charge to move the node appreciably) does the circuit fail to oscillate: the heavily-loaded node is then frozen at its initial voltage and the loop is locked in the metastable state.

answers.question: If we double the widths of the NMOS and PMOS devices in Figure 7, what happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
Doubling the width of every NMOS- and PMOS-device gives you twice as much channel area while the supply voltage is left unchanged.  
The main consequences are

1. Transconductance, gm, roughly doubles.  
   Thermal-noise voltage referred to the gate ≈ 4kT γ /gm therefore falls by 2.  
   (1/f noise also drops by ≈2 because the device area is doubled.)

2. The gate-to-gate capacitance that each stage has to drive also doubles.  
   At the same time the effective on-resistance of the driver is cut in half, so the RC
   delay of every inverter – and hence the oscillation frequency – stays almost the same
   (R/2 × 2C ≈ constant).

3. Dynamic power dissipation rises in proportion to the capacitance:
      Pdyn = C VDD² f  ⟹ 2 C → 2 P.  

In Leeson-type or Hajimiri-analyses of ring oscillators the single-sideband phase-noise
density is approximately

      L(Δf) ∝ (FkT) / (2 Psig)

so doubling the signal power (or, equivalently, the energy per cycle) divides the
phase-noise number by two.

Result: The phase-noise power density is cut in half, i.e. it improves by about 3 dB over the whole offset-frequency range (thermal as well as 1/f regions).

What changes when you make every NMOS and PMOS twice as wide

1. Transconductance and switching current  
   gm  ∝ W and the static / dynamic current roughly double, so the white channel-noise current density (4kTγgm) doubles.

2. Node capacitances  
   All gate-, diffusion- and wiring-capacitances also scale with W, so every internal node capacitance doubles.

3. Energy stored in the “tank” of the ring  
   The total electrical energy per stage, ½ CVDD², therefore doubles.

4. Phase perturbation produced by a given noise current  
   A noise-current impulse delivers the same charge, but that charge is now spread over 2 × the capacitance, so the resulting voltage (and therefore time/phase) disturbance is cut in half.  
   From the Hajimiri–Lee point of view σφ² ∝ kT/E; doubling E halves σφ².

Result

The single-sideband phase-noise power density L{Δf} is inversely proportional to the stored energy (or to the power being dissipated).  
E (and the average power) has doubled, so L{Δf} is reduced by a factor of 2, i.e. about 3 dB.

answers.question:
Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in Figure 8.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
and use `f0` for the oscillation frequency.

answer.text:
Every time an internal node of the ring oscillator changes logic state the load-capacitor CL either:

• receives a charge +CL VDD from the supply (low → high), or  
• returns the same charge to ground (high → low).

Energy taken from the supply for one transition  

 Etr = ½ CL VDD²  

and there are two transitions per oscillation period T = 1/f0, so the energy drawn per node each period is  

 Eper node = CL VDD².

Average power drawn by one node  

 Pnode = Eper node / T = CL VDD² f0.

With the three inverters of Fig. 8 the total dynamic power is  

 Ptot = 3 CL VDD² f0.

Average supply current  

 Iavg = Ptot / VDD = 3 CL VDD f0.

The small-signal (incremental) resistance seen when looking into the supply node is therefore  

 Rx = dVDD / dIavg = VDD / Iavg = 1 / (3 CL f0).

(For a general N-stage ring oscillator, Rx = 1 / (N CL f0).)

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies oscillation-driven charging of the three load capacitances and derives the expected supply resistance, Rx ≈ 1/(3 CL f0), with f0 treated as fixed.

   QRise  = C_L · VDD

   With three nodes, the total charge taken from the supply in one period is  
   QPER = 3 · C_L · VDD

3. Average (dc) supply current  
   IAVG = QPER / T = 3 · C_L · VDD · f0

4. Small-signal conductance seen at the supply node  
   Gx = dIAVG / dVDD = 3 · C_L · f0

5. Hence the small-signal resistance Rx is the reciprocal of this conductance  

     Rx = 1 / Gx = 1 / (3 · C_L · f0)

Generalising, an N-stage ring oscillator presents  

     Rx = 1 / (N · C_L · f0)

and for the three-stage circuit of Fig. 8 the result is

     Rx = 1 / (3 C_L f0).

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in Figure 8, consider the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
`f0` for the oscillation frequency, and `TD` for the delay of one inverter stage.

From the dynamic charging and discharging of the three load capacitances, one
can write

```text
RX ~= 1 / (3 f0 CL)
```

Somebody then argues that, because the circuit is oscillating, the path from
`VDD` to ground through the transistors is off for much of the cycle, so the
average resistance should be much higher than the MOS on-resistance or inverse
transconductance scale.

Do you agree with this argument?

answer.text:
No.

The quantity RX that we are talking about is the small-signal (low-frequency) resistance seen at the VDD pin, i.e.  

RX = dVDD / dIAVG ,

where IAVG is the cycle-average current that the ring oscillator draws from the supply.  
For a three-stage ring, every period T0 = 1 / f0 each node makes one 0 → VDD or VDD → 0 transition, so in every cycle

total charge taken from the supply  Q = 3 CL VDD .

Consequently  

IAVG = Q / T0 = 3 CL VDD f0 ,

and a small perturbation ΔVDD changes that average current by  

ΔI = 3 CL f0 ΔVDD .

Therefore  

RX = ΔVDD / ΔI = 1 / (3 CL f0)

as stated.

What matters is the charge that has to be delivered every cycle, not whether the
transistor path between VDD and ground is continuously on.  
During the short switching interval the devices are strongly on and draw large
current pulses; during the rest of the period they draw virtually none.  The
above derivation already averages over that duty cycle through the 1/f0 factor.
Hence the fact that “the path is off for much of the cycle” does not make RX
large; it is already accounted for.

For typical values (CL ≈ 50 fF, f0 ≈ 200 MHz)  

RX ≈ 1 / (3·200 M·50 fF) ≈ 33 kΩ,

which is only a few-to-ten times the on-resistance of a minimum-size CMOS
device—not orders of magnitude larger.  Short-circuit (crowbar) current that
flows while both pull-up and pull-down devices are momentarily on actually
reduces RX further.

Hence the argument that the effective resistance must be “much higher” than the
MOS on-resistance is incorrect; the simple dynamic analysis leading to
RX ≈ 1/(3 f0 CL) is the right way to view the supply impedance of the
oscillating ring.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly rejects the claim and uses the cycle-averaged charging current to show that the off-time is already accounted for in RX ≈ 1/(3 f0 CL). It also explicitly places RX within a few-to-ten times the MOS on-resistance scale, satisfying the full-credit rule.

answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 9, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:

answers.question:
For the divide-by-two topology in Figure 11, does the speed improve or degrade
if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors, i.e. the transistors whose
gates are driven by `CK` or `CKbar`?

answer.text:
Widening the devices that are driven by CK / CK̄ does not make the divider faster; it usually makes it slower.

Why?

1. When a clocked device is ON, the delay of the path that includes it is roughly  
   t ≈ Ron · Cnode ,  
   where Ron ≈ 1/W and Cnode contains the transistor’s own diffusion capacitance, which is ≈ W.  
   Therefore Ron·Cnode is almost independent of W; enlarging the device does not shorten this intrinsic
   RC time-constant.

2. What does grow with W is the capacitance seen by the clock (gate Cg + diffusion to the clock rail).  
   The clock driver now has to charge/discharge a larger load, so the CK/CK̄ edges become slower.  
   Every internal operation in the divider is initiated or terminated by one of these edges, so the
   overall cycle time increases.

3. The additional diffusion capacitance of the wider devices also appears on the storage nodes,
   increasing the load that the cross-coupled devices must drive; any benefit obtained from the
   lower Ron is more than cancelled by this extra capacitance.

Hence making the CK-controlled transistors wider provides little or no reduction in the internal
RC delay but definitely penalises the clock edge rate, so the maximum operating frequency degrades.
For highest speed these transistors are normally kept at (or close to) minimum width.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer reaches the opposite of the topology-specific result: widening the clocked devices improves speed by lowering series resistance while adding little loading to the data path. Charge sharing degrades swing but is acceptable up to a point; the claimed slowdown from the start earns 1.

For the divide-by-two topology in Figure 11, does the speed improve or degrade
if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors, i.e. the transistors whose
gates are driven by `CK` or `CKbar`?

answer.text:
In this ÷2 cell the “clocked” devices act only as pass-transistors that open and close the current path; they do not actively pull the internal nodes up or down—that job is done by the cross-coupled pull-up/pull-down transistors.  

If we make the clocked devices wider:

1. Their on-resistance (≈1/W) gets smaller, so the path they form becomes slightly better.
2. But their gate capacitance and their source / drain diffusion capacitances grow in direct proportion to W.

The extra capacitance shows up in two places that matter for speed:  
• on the clock lines CK / CK̅, which now have a heavier load to charge and discharge, and  
• on the two internal storage nodes, which the cross-coupled devices must drive even though those devices have not been strengthened.

Once the pass-transistor resistance is low enough that it is no longer the dominant term in the delay, any further reduction in R gives almost no benefit, whereas the added C slows both the clock edges and the node transitions. Therefore, enlarging the clocked transistors beyond the minimum (or near-minimum) size causes the overall propagation delay to increase, i.e. the maximum toggle frequency goes down.

So: after a small optimum point, increasing the widths of the transistors driven by CK/CK̅ degrades, rather than improves, the speed of the divide-by-two stage.

In this topology the devices add little loading to the data path; speed improves considerably, while charge sharing degrades swing only acceptably up to a point.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
Figure 12(a) is nothing more than a dynamic D-latch whose own output is fed back to its input.  
Give the main nodes the names shown below and follow one clock period.

                    CK=1           CK=0
      ──┬── T1 ON, T2 OFF ──┬── T1 OFF, T2 ON ──
 Q ──T1──► A ─Inv1─► B   (isolated)  │
 │                         │          │
 │<── Inv4 ◄── Inv3 ◄── Inv2 ◄─T2◄────┘
 └──────────────────────────────────────┘   (feedback wire)

1. Φ1 : CK = 1  
   • T1 is ON, so the present value that exists on Q is copied to node A.  
   • Inv1 inverts it and places ¬Q on node B.  
   • T2 is OFF, therefore B is cut off from the rest of the loop and merely holds the sampled value on its parasitic capacitance.

2. Φ2 : CK = 0  
   • T1 turns OFF, freezing node A.  
   • T2 turns ON, so the content of B is released into the delay line made of Inv2-Inv3-Inv4 and finally reaches Q.  
   • Between B and Q there are three inversions (Inv2-Inv3-Inv4), i.e. an odd number, so the signal that reaches Q is ¬(¬Q) = Q itself – the very level that Q already had.

Hence, after the whole clock cycle the voltage on Q has not changed; the circuit simply regenerates (retains) its previous logic state. In other words

     D = Q      (because the loop contains an even number – four – of inversions)

so the arrangement of Fig. 12(a) is only a “remember” latch and it cannot divide the clock by two.

To obtain a toggle (T-flip-flop) and thus an fCLK/2 output, the feedback must supply the complement of Q to the latch input, i.e.

     D = ¬Q .

That is achieved in Fig. 12(b) by inserting one extra inverter (shown in red) in the feedback path, making the total number of inversions around the loop five (odd). With that single change the node Q changes state every complete clock period, giving the required divide-by-two action.
