The inversion and feedback analysis therefore misidentifies its operation.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
Let  

 TG1 = the pass-gate that is controlled by CK  
 TG2 = the pass-gate that is controlled by ĆK (CK̅)  
 A  = node at the input of INV1 (output of TG1)  
 B  = output of INV1 / input of TG2  
 Q  = output of the last inverter (the signal that is to be divided)

There are a total of three inverters between node B and the final output Q, so the
loop that is closed through the two transmission gates contains an odd number of
inversions.

Operation is split in the two non-overlapping clock phases:

1. CK = 1  (“sample” phase)  
   • TG1 is ON, TG2 is OFF – the loop is opened just after INV1.  
   • Q is passed through TG1 and INV1, therefore  
     B = ¬Q.  
   • Because TG2 is open, the new value present on node B cannot yet propagate
     further round the loop; Q itself therefore remains unchanged during this half
     cycle.  
   • In other words, while CK = 1 the circuit prepares (pre-computes) the complement
     of the present state and stores it on the dynamic node B.

2. CK = 0  (“hold / evaluate” phase)  
   • TG1 turns OFF and isolates node A, while TG2 turns ON and closes the feedback
     path.  
   • B is now connected to the input of the remaining chain of three inverters, so
     after those three inversions reach steady state the value that appears at the
     output is  

     Qnew = (¬)³ B = ¬B = ¬(¬Qold) = ¬Qold.  

   • Thus Q toggles once during every low half-cycle of the clock.  
   • With TG2 ON the latch now holds the new value; when the clock goes high again
     the whole sequence repeats.

Because one complete period of Q requires two consecutive half cycles of the
external clock, the frequency seen at node Q is exactly one half of the clock
frequency.  Stated differently, the circuit behaves as a T-flip-flop (toggle
flip-flop) driven by CK:

     Q ← ¬Q   at every falling edge of CK ⇒ fQ = fCK ⁄ 2

Important observations

•  The arrangement is nothing more than a dynamic latch whose data input is tied
   to its own output through an odd number of inverters; by alternately opening
   and closing the two complementary transmission gates the latch first samples
   the present state and then reinserts that value (after an odd inversion) as the
   new state – hence the automatic toggle action.

•  The three inverters in the feedback path supply the necessary odd inversion,
   restore full logic levels, and provide adequate delay so that the value on the
   dynamic node B is fully resolved before it is re-captured.

•  Since node B is a dynamic (capacitive) node it must be refreshed every clock
   period; therefore the clock may not be stopped, and its lowest permissible
   frequency is set by the leakage on that node.

Thus Figure 12(a) realises a single-phase, very compact, dynamic divide-by-two
circuit.

However, the detailed state update is inconsistent: if B = ¬Qold, then three inversions give Qnew = ¬B = Qold, not ¬Qold, so the feedback derivation does not support the stated toggle.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
Figure 12(a) is nothing more mysterious than a dynamic T-flip-flop—i.e. a latch that toggles every time it is clocked and therefore delivers CK / 2.

How it is put together

1. Two transmission-gate (or single-MOS) switches  
   • the left–hand one is driven by CK  
   • the right–hand one is driven by  CK̅  
2. A chain containing an odd number of inverters (three are shown).

Label the nodes  

 X – the small node immediately to the right of the CK-controlled switch  
 Y – output of INV₁  
 Z – output of the last inverter, taken as Q and fed back to the CK switch.

Operation

CK = 1  (evaluate phase)  
• The left switch is ON, the right one is OFF.  
• Node X is shorted to Z, so the logic level that was stored during the previous half-cycle is presented to the input of INV₁.  
• Because the loop contains an odd number of inversions (INV₁ + the two that follow), after one propagation delay what appears at Z is the complement of the level that had been stored.  
 → during the high phase the circuit computes ¬Q(prev).

CK = 0  (store phase)  
• The left switch turns OFF; the right switch turns ON.  
• The loop now closes through an odd number of inversions; the new value generated during the evaluate phase is therefore self-consistent and is held statically (actually pseudo-statically—the node X is only capacitively stored, so very low clock rates are limited by leakage).  
 → the value produced in the last high phase is preserved until the next high phase.

Thus each full clock period produces exactly one toggle of Z:

 Q(next) = ¬Q(now)

and the waveform at Z (or any other odd-inverter tap) is a square wave at half the clock frequency.

Figure 12(b) simply redraws the active path during CK = 1 (shown in red) to emphasise that one more inversion is inserted before the feedback, making the complement that forces the toggle.

Practical notes

• Because X is a dynamic (capacitive) node the clock cannot be allowed to stay low for arbitrarily long—otherwise charge leaks away and the state is lost.  
• The highest usable clock frequency is limited by the propagation delay of the three-inverter path.  
• Fan-out must be taken from the final buffered inverter(s); loading node X would disturb the dynamic storage.

In short, Figure 12(a) realises a compact dynamic divide-by-two (T-flip-flop) built from a transmission-gate latch plus an odd delay line.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the arrangement as a dynamic-latch divide-by-two circuit and explains that clocked feedback toggling produces an output at CK/2. It also recognizes dynamic charge storage and leakage; the more specific inverter-path details are secondary under the golden solution.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in Figure 12(b) affect the performance?

answer.text:
The extra (red) inverter is just a buffer.  
In the original circuit (a) the first inverter ­Inv1 has to drive

• the gate capacitance of the large transmission gate that is controlled by 𝑪K̅,  
• the long piece of interconnect that closes the ring, and  
• the three inverters that follow it.

That is a very heavy fan-out, so the propagation delay through Inv1 dominates the
clock-to-output delay of the whole loop.

In (b) the red inverter is inserted between Inv1 and that heavy load:

Inv1 → small load (input of the red inverter)  
red inverter → large load (transmission-gate gate + wire + the rest of the inverters)

Thus the total load is split over two stages.  Using logical-effort terminology we
have replaced one stage with a large fan-out F by two stages each driving roughly √F,
which gives a noticeably smaller total delay even though one intrinsic gate delay
has been added.  Consequently

• the critical path is shorter in time, so the ring (or the latch, flip-flop, etc.)
  can operate at a higher clock frequency;  
• Inv1 no longer sees the large capacitive load, so its transition edges are
  steeper, further improving speed;  
• the only penalties are one extra inverter of area/power and the small extra input
  capacitance that that inverter adds to the clock net.

In short, the red inverter improves performance (higher maximum frequency /
shorter clock-to-Q delay) at the cost of one additional gate and a slight increase
in clock loading.

answer.text:
The extra (red) inverter is placed immediately after the transmission-gate switch that is controlled by CK.  
Because of it,

1. The transmission gate now has to drive only the small gate capacitance of one inverter instead of the long wire plus the inputs of the three following inverters.  
   Rtg · Cload (large)  →  Rtg · Cin(inv)  (very small)

2. The red inverter, which is connected to the full supply rails, re-buffers the signal and drives the heavy load itself.  
   • Restores full-swing levels (removes the Vth drop of the pass device).  
   • Gives a low-resistance pull-up / pull-down path for the large load.

3. When CK goes low and the transmission gate opens, the red inverter also provides a local feedback path that keeps the internal node from floating, so the stored value is held more robustly and with less leakage.

The net result is

• Shorter CK-to-Q delay / higher maximum frequency.  
• Smaller dynamic power in the pass device.  
• Better noise-margin and data-retention when the gate is open.

In other words, adding the red inverter isolates the high-resistance switch from a large capacitive load and restores the logic level, which makes the circuit markedly faster and more reliable.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in Figure 12(b) affect the performance?

answer.text:
The extra (red) inverter that is placed between the two clock-controlled breaks in Fig 12(b) works as a local buffer for the internal loop node.

1. When CK is HIGH (latch transparent)  
   • The first transmission gate is ON and has to charge/discharge only the input capacitance of the red inverter, not the long string of inverters that form the rest of the loop.  
   • The effective fan-out of the clocked device therefore drops sharply, so the CK→node delay as well as the dynamic power drawn from the clock is reduced.

2. When CK goes LOW (latch in hold)  
   • The first transmission gate turns OFF, the second one (/CK) turns ON and the red inverter closes a short, odd-inversion feedback path.  
   • This regenerates the value that was present on the internal node and keeps it solid while the latch is closed (better noise margin and data retention).

Cost: the only price paid is the extra gate capacitance that the red inverter adds to the node it is connected to, which produces a very small additional delay after the first inverter.  
Benefit: the load removed from the clocked pass device is much larger than the load added to the data path, so the net effect is a faster, lower-power, and more robust latch.

In short, the red inverter isolates the clocked switch from a large capacitive load and provides regenerative storage; the overall propagation delay is reduced and the maximum operating frequency is increased.

   – The transmission gate in front of Inv1 is on; the data coming from the previous stage strongly drives the node.

Nothing that the red inverter is connected to can hold a data node, therefore it cannot act as a “keeper” and it certainly does not form a cross-coupled pair with Inv1.

What the drawing shows is simply the generation (and buffering) of the complementary clock:

• The input of the red inverter is the clock CK.  
• Its output drives the line labelled  CK̅ , the control signal for the second transmission gate that sits on the output of Inv1.  
• Because the inverter is in the clock path and not in the data path, when the two transmission-gate switches are open the red inverter is completely isolated from the stored node. It has no way to refresh the charge that is left on that node while the clock is low. The latch therefore remains a dynamic latch and still needs to be re-evaluated often enough to overcome leakage.

Placing the inverter locally has two practical purposes:

1. It avoids having to distribute both CK and CK̅ over long wiring; only CK is brought in and its complement is generated on the spot.  
2. The delay through the inverter introduces a small non-overlap (dead-time) between the two control signals, guaranteeing that the two transmission gates are never simultaneously on.

So the red inverter is part of the clock-distribution network, not a data keeper; it does not eliminate the minimum-frequency requirement of the dynamic latch.

answers.question:
In Figure 12(b), somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

But the input of the red inverter is not tied to the output of `Inv1`.

answer.text:
The answer you quoted is basically correct – the red inverter is added only so that the node that is left floating in Fig-12(a) becomes a static node in Fig-12(b).  
What sometimes causes confusion is the exact wiring, so let us label the three relevant nodes in Fig-12(b).

  • XA -– node between the CK-controlled transmission gate and the input of Inv1  
  • Y  -– output of Inv1 (this node is on the right-hand side of Inv1)  
  • XB -– node on the right-hand side of the 𝘊𝘒̅ transmission gate (this is simply the continuation of the ring)

In Fig-12(b) the extra inverter is connected from Y back to XA:

 Y (output of Inv1) → red inverter → XA (input of Inv1)

Hence, when the 𝘊𝘒̅ transmission gate is ON (CK = 0), nodes Y and XB are shorted together and the red inverter really does “see” the output of Inv1.  
When CK goes high again that gate opens, XA is isolated from the rest of the ring, and the only element that can keep XA from drifting away is the weak red inverter. Together with Inv1 it now forms a two-inverter feedback loop (XA → Inv1 → Y → red inv → XA), i.e. a static cross-coupled latch. Because that loop is regenerative, it will restore any small leakage-induced disturbance on XA; therefore the data stored in the master section no longer fades away and the minimum-clock-frequency requirement disappears.

Why must the red inverter be weak?  
During the other half of the cycle (CK = 1) the CK-controlled transmission gate is ON and the ring is driving XA directly. The red inverter must be too weak to fight that strong driver, otherwise it would cause contention. A very small p-device and n-device (or a stacked device) is therefore used – this is exactly the “keeper” used in domino logic.

So:

1. Yes, the red inverter is acting as a keeper.  
2. It does form a latch with Inv1; the fact that the connection passes through the 𝘊𝘒̅ transmission gate simply guarantees that the keeper is disabled while the node is being actively written.  
3. Its purpose is to turn the purely dynamic master node in Fig-12(a) into a static one, eliminating the minimum-frequency constraint that Fig-12(a) suffers from.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
With the feedback topology of Fig. 13 the two quantities that determine the noise figure (NF) are

1. the transconductance of the input device, gm1 , and  
2. the value of the feedback resistor, RF .

All the other circuit elements only fix the small-signal voltage gain (Av ≃ –gm1∙Ro) that appears between the drain and the gate.

A.   Input impedance constraint  
For the shunt-feedback amplifier the input resistance is

  Rin = RF /(1 + Av) ≃ RF /(1 + gm1∙Ro)    (1)

and it must be 50 Ω.  Equation (1) therefore ties RF to gm1 (and to the intrinsic gain gm1∙Ro):

  RF = 50 Ω · (1 + gm1∙Ro)         (2)

B.   Noise figure expression  
If only the channel (γ ≈ 2⁄3) and thermal-noise of the feedback resistor are considered, the input-referred noise voltage density is

  e²n,total = 4kT·50 Ω                       (source)  
     + 4kT·γ/gm1                       (M1 channel)  
     + 4kT·RF /(1 + Av)² = 4kT·50 Ω /RF   (feedback-resistor)

Dividing the total noise by the source noise (4kT·50 Ω) gives

  F = 1 + γ /(gm1·50 Ω) + 50 Ω /RF    (3)

Using (2) in (3) yields

  F = 1 + γ /(gm1·50 Ω) + 1 /(1 + gm1·Ro)  (4)

C.   What minimises F while Rin = 50 Ω ?  

• The second term, γ /(gm1·50 Ω), decreases monotonically with gm1.  
• The third term, 1 /(1 + gm1·Ro), also decreases monotonically with gm1 (because gm1 raises the open-loop gain and therefore allows a larger RF).

Consequently F is a strictly decreasing function of gm1; the smallest NF is obtained when gm1 (and hence gm1·Ro) is made as large as the power budget and the technology allow.

D.   Practical design recipe  

1. Bias M1 at the highest current density that the allowed supply current permits and choose a large W/L so that gm1 is as large as possible.  
2. Use a cascode or another high-output-resistance load for M1 so that Ro is large, further enlarging gm1·Ro.  
3. Having obtained gm1 and Av, set  
  RF = 50 Ω · (1 + |Av|) ≃ 50 Ω · (1 + gm1·Ro)  
   so that Rin remains exactly 50 Ω.  
4. If additional gate-noise or flicker-noise terms must be taken into account the optimum gm1 still lies at the highest practical value; the calculated NF will settle at a floor determined by technology (≈1.2–1.5 dB in modern CMOS).

In short: to optimise the circuit for minimum noise figure while keeping Rin = 50 Ω, maximise the open-loop gain by running the input transistor with the largest feasible gm (and intrinsic gain), then choose the feedback resistor from (2).  The larger gm simultaneously lowers the transistor’s own noise and allows a larger RF, which suppresses the noise contribution of the feedback resistor, yielding the lowest attainable NF for the given power dissipation.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
In the resistive-feedback LNA of Fig. 13 there are only two quantities that determine both

• the input resistance   
• the input-referred thermal noise

namely

 1. the trans-conductance of the input transistor, g m1  
 2. the feedback resistor, R F                   

(All other elements – the coupling capacitor C 1 and the cascode device M 2 – do not influence the
low-frequency value of R in and only make a second–order contribution to the noise.)

────────────────────────────────────────
1 Relations that have to be satisfied
────────────────────────────────────────
Input resistance (small-signal, ro  ≫ R F)

     R in  =  1 / g m1    ‖    R F /(1+|A v |)         (1)

where A v  ≈ –g m1 R L is the open-loop gain seen by the feedback network
(R L is the drain load, realised with the current source M 2 ‖ r o1 ‖ r o2 ).

Noise factor referred to the 50 Ω source, R S = 50 Ω:

     F  ≈  1  +  γ /(g m1 R S )   +  R S /R F              (2)

(γ ≃ 2/3 in long-channel CMOS; the small contribution of M 2 has been
neglected because it can easily be made < 0.1 dB by choosing a small device.)

Equation (2) shows that
• the term γ /(g m1 R S ) falls when g m1 is increased, and  
• the term R S /R F falls when R F is increased.

────────────────────────────────────────
2 Design strategy (keep R in = 50 Ω, minimise F)
────────────────────────────────────────
Step 1  Choose the largest g m1 that the supply-voltage head-room,
power budget and bandwidth will allow.
          – For a 50 Ω interface, g m1 must at least exceed 1/50 Ω ≃ 20 mS;  
            practically, pick g m1 ≥ 3–5 × (1/50 Ω) to obtain a good NF.

Step 2  Calculate the open-loop gain |A v | = g m1 R L obtained with the
chosen bias current and load impedance R L .

Step 3  With this g m1 and A v , compute the feedback resistor that
re-establishes the 50 Ω match by rearranging (1):

     R F  =  50 Ω · (1 + |A v |) / (1 – 50 Ω · g m1)        (3)

          (The denominator is positive because g m1 has been chosen
           larger than 1/50 Ω.)

Step 4  Verify the resulting noise figure with (2):

     F ≈ 1 + γ /(g m1 · 50 Ω) + 50 Ω / R F

          If F is still higher than the specification, go back to Step 1
          and increase g m1 (which automatically lets R F become larger
          through (3), further lowering its noise contribution).

Step 5  Make the cascode device M 2 just large enough to keep the
required gain and voltage head-room; a small g m2 keeps its own
thermal noise negligible.

────────────────────────────────────────
3 What the procedure does
────────────────────────────────────────
• Raising g m1 lowers the transistor-channel noise (second term of (2)).  
• Because g m1 has gone up, equation (3) forces R F to increase, so the
  thermal noise of the feedback resistor (third term of (2)) also falls.  
• The 50 Ω power match is preserved at every iteration because we
  recalculate R F from (3).

Since both noise-producing terms decrease monotonically with g m1 ,
the minimum NF is always obtained at the highest g m1 (hence highest
bias current or widest device) that the system can tolerate.
In modern CMOS processes this procedure yields, for a
perfect 50 Ω match, noise figures of roughly 2 dB with only a few mW
of dc power.

So, to optimise the circuit for minimum NF while keeping R in = 50 Ω
you simply

• make g m1 as large as practicable, and  
• readjust R F with equation (3);

all other parameters (device length, M 2 size, etc.) are then chosen
for gain and bandwidth, as their influence on the NF is secondary.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
Start from the two relations that completely describe the feedback-matched stage

1.  Input resistance  
       Rin = RF /(1 + gm RF)

2.  Small–signal noise factor (thermal noise only, flicker ignored)  

       F = 1 + γ/(gm Rin) + Rin / RF                       ( γ ≈ 2/3 in long channel MOS )

Put Rin = 50 Ω.  
From (1)

          RF = 50 Ω /(1 – gm · 50 Ω)           (gm < 1/50 Ω = 20 mS so that RF is positive)

Eliminate RF in (2):

          F = 1 + γ/(gm · 50 Ω) + 1 – gm · 50 Ω
            = 2 + γ/(gm · 50 Ω) – gm · 50 Ω

Hence F is a one-parameter function of gm only.  
dF / dgm = –γ/(gm² · 50 Ω) – 50 Ω < 0   for every admissible gm,  
so F decreases monotonically as gm increases and attains its minimum when gm approaches its maximum allowed value, i.e.

          gm → 1 / 50 Ω  (≈ 20 mS)  ⇒  RF → ∞

The theoretical minimum noise factor is therefore

          Fmin = 1 + γ     ( ≃ 1.6 … 1.8 ⇒ 1.8–2.3 dB )

In practice we pick gm a few per-cent below 1/50 Ω (say 18–19 mS) so that RF is a few-hundred Ω to a few-kΩ—large enough to make its Johnson noise negligible, yet still realisable on chip.

Design procedure for minimum NF with the 50-Ω constraint

1. Increase the width and/or bias current of M1 until gm is as high as power-budget and head-room allow, but keep gm < 20 mS.  
2. Compute the feedback resistor from RF = 50 /(1 – 50·gm).  
3. Make C1 large so that its reactance is small in the band of interest.  
4. Use a large, low-noise load device (M2) or a cascode so that its noise is not reflected to the input.  

Because Rin is fixed at 50 Ω, the only effective knob for NF is gm; the optimum NF is obtained simply by pushing gm as high as possible and increasing RF accordingly. No further trade-off is available in this topology.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in Figure 14(a).

answer.text:
With the photodiode (or any other current source) connected to node P we are interested in the small-signal ratio  

 Zin = VP / Iin

where Iin is the current driven into the circuit and VP is the resulting voltage that appears at the external pin P.

1.  Replace the transistor amplifier by the low-frequency model shown in Fig. 14 (b):  
 • the inverting input node is V1,  
 • the amplifier produces the output −A V1,  
 • RF is returned from the output to V1,  
 • the output sees the load RD2,  
 • the only element that lies between the external pin and the inverting input is the (very large) amplifier input resistance Rin.

2.  Write the KCL equation at the inverting input node V1  

 (VP − V1)/Rin + (Vout − V1)/RF  = 0 .

3.  Substitute the amplifier relation Vout = −A V1  

 (VP − V1)/Rin  = (A+1) V1 / RF .     (1)

4.  The current entering the circuit is the current through Rin  

 Iin = (VP − V1)/Rin.                 (2)

5.  Eliminate (VP − V1)/Rin between (1) and (2) and solve for VP/Iin:

 Iin                = (A+1) V1 / RF                        
 VP                = V1[1 + Rin(A+1)/RF]                  

 ⇒ Zin = VP/Iin = Rin + RF /(A+1).                        (3)

Because the MOS gate is practically an open circuit, Rin is orders of magnitude larger than the other resistances and can be neglected.  Thus

 Zin ≈ RF /(1 + A)  ≃ RF /A  for |A| ≫ 1.            (4)

Open-loop gain of the transistor realisation  
Ignoring channel-length modulation and assuming M2 merely relays the current, the low-frequency voltage gain of Fig. 14 (a) is approximately

 A ≈ gm1 RD1 · gm3 RD2  (negative sign omitted in magnitude).

Hence the input impedance of the complete TIA is

 Zin ≈  RF /[1 + gm1 RD1 gm3 RD2]     
     ≈  RF /(gm1 RD1 gm3 RD2)      when gm1 RD1 gm3 RD2 ≫ 1.

Typical values (gm ≈ 5 mS, RD ≈ 10 kΩ, RF ≈ 10 kΩ) give a loop gain of a few thousand and an input impedance of only a few ohms, so node P behaves almost like a virtual ground – exactly the requirement for an effective transimpedance amplifier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It recognizes that feedback lowers the input impedance to roughly RF/A at high gain, but its model omits the output-side resistance in the exact Miller result and gives an incorrect gain expression. The required result is (RF + RD2)/(1 + A0), with A0 = (1/2)gm1 gm2,3 RD1 RD2.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in Figure 14(a).

answer.text:
Denote by V1 the small-signal voltage that appears at the input node P, and by Iin the small-signal current that is forced into that node.  
From the simplified model of Fig. 14(b)

• A resistor Rin connects the node to ground.  
• A feedback resistor RF connects the node to the amplifier output.  
• The amplifier produces the voltage  
  Vout = –A V1 .

1.  Write KCL at node P (node voltage = V1):

       Iin = V1 / Rin + (V1 – Vout) / RF                (1)

2.  Substitute Vout = –A V1 into (1):

       Iin = V1 / Rin + (V1 + A V1) / RF  
            = V1 [ 1 / Rin + (1 + A) / RF ]            (2)

3.  The small-signal input impedance is

       Zin ≡ V1 / Iin  
            = 1 / [ 1 / Rin + (1 + A) / RF ]  
            = ( Rin RF ) / [ RF + (1 + A) Rin ]        (3)

4.  In most practical TIAs Rin is comparatively large and the loop-gain term A is very large, so RF ≪ (1 + A) Rin.  
  Under this usual condition,

       Zin ≈ RF / (1 + A) ≈ RF / A                     (4)

Hence the feedback around the high-gain stage forces the input node to a very low impedance—approximately the feedback resistor divided by the open-loop gain of the internal amplifier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly recognizes that feedback lowers the input impedance and gives the familiar approximate RF/(1+A) relation. But it substitutes a different simplified model and omits the output-side RD2 contribution, so it misses the required result (RF+RD2)/(1+A0) and the specified unloaded gain.

answers.question: Compute the input impedance of the circuit in Figure 14(a).

answer.text:
At the signal node P the diode current Iin has only one low-impedance path to ground: through the feedback resistor RF.  
The voltage amplifier that follows M1 senses the voltage at P (call it V1 ) and, with an open-loop gain −A, drives the right-hand end of RF to the voltage  

  Vo =  −A V1 .  

Hence the current that flows through RF is  

  Iin = (V1  −  Vo)/RF = (V1  − (−A V1 ))/RF = (1 + A) V1 /RF .  

The small-signal input impedance Rin is the ratio of the node-voltage to the injected current:

  Rin = V1 /Iin = RF /(1 + A) .   (1)

If the open-loop gain is large (|A| ≫ 1),

  Rin ≈ RF /|A|  ≪ RF .

For the transistor implementation of Fig. 14(a) the low-frequency open-loop gain is, to first order,

  A ≈ −gm1 RD1 gm2 RD2 ,  

so that

  Rin ≈ RF /(1 + gm1 RD1 gm2 RD2 )  ≈ RF /(gm1 RD1 gm2 RD2)  (for large gain).

Thus the feedback reduces the input resistance by the loop-gain factor, giving the very low input impedance required of a wide-band transimpedance amplifier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer correctly recognizes that feedback lowers the input resistance, but its computed expression omits the output-side resistance: the exact result is Rin = (RF + RD2)/(1 + A0). It also gives an incorrect gain expression, missing the factor of 1/2 and the gm2,3 definition.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Treat the noise that the regulator adds to its output,  
vout(t)=VDD + nv(t) , with one–sided power–spectral density Svout(f)=Sth(f) [V²/Hz],  
as a small perturbation of the VCO supply.

1. Supply-to-frequency sensitivity  
   Kvdd = ∂fosc / ∂Vout [Hz / V]          (obtain from a dc or transient sweep of the VCO versus Vout).

2. From supply noise to frequency noise  
   Δf(t)=Kvdd nv(t)  ⇒ PSD of the frequency fluctuations  
   Sf(f)=Kvdd² Sth(f) [Hz²/Hz].

3. Frequency noise → phase noise  
   The oscillator phase is the time integral of the frequency error:  
   φ(t)=∫2π Δf(t)dt → in the frequency domain Φ(f)=Kvdd Vout(f)/(j f).  
   Hence the phase-noise PSD is  

   Sφ(f)= Kvdd² Sth(f) / f² [rad²/Hz].

4. Single-sideband (SSB) phase-noise in the usual dBc/Hz notation  
   L(f)=½ Sφ(f)= Kvdd² Sth(f) / (2 f²) [dBc/Hz before taking 10 log₁₀].

So the LDO-originated contribution at an offset foff from the carrier is

L(foff)=10 log₁₀ [ Kvdd² Sth(foff) / (2 foff²) ]  dBc/Hz.

Procedure to evaluate it:

• Simulate/measure the VCO and extract Kvdd.  
• Use the LDO output-noise spectrum Sth(f).  
• Insert both in the expression above and convert to dBc/Hz.

If Sth is flat (thermal noise), the resulting phase noise falls with 20 dB/decade of offset frequency.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The supply-to-frequency sensitivity and FM-to-phase-noise conversion are correctly derived, including the 1/foff² dependence and SSB expression. It omits the circuit-specific insight that supply noise acts directly on the varactors, making Kpush closely related to KVCO.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Step 1 – write the supply noise that reaches the VCO  
The LDO output can be written as  

  Vout(t) = VDD,dc + vn(t)           with   Svout(f) = Sth  [V²/Hz] (white thermal noise)

Step 2 – relate supply-voltage variations to instantaneous-frequency variations  
For every oscillator there is a “supply pushing” coefficient

  kVDD = ∂ω0 / ∂Vout  [rad s⁻¹ V⁻¹]                (or in Hz / V)

so that a small supply disturbance produces a frequency disturbance

  δω(t) = kVDD · vn(t)

Step 3 – convert the frequency disturbance to a phase disturbance  
Phase is the time integral of frequency:

  δφ(t) = ∫ δω(t) dt = kVDD ∫ vn(t) dt

Transforming to the frequency domain (Ω = 2πf):

  Φ(jΩ) = kVDD · Vn(jΩ) / (jΩ)

Hence the transfer function from supply noise to phase is  

  Hφvdd(jΩ) = kVDD / (jΩ)

Step 4 – obtain the phase-noise power spectral density  
Two-sided phase-noise PSD:

  Sφ(Ω) = |Hφvdd(jΩ)|² · Svout(Ω)
           = kVDD² · Sth / Ω²

Re-writing with offset frequency f = Ω / 2π:

  Sφ(f) = kVDD² · Sth / (2πf)²                (rad²/Hz)

Step 5 – single-sideband phase noise usually quoted for oscillators  

  L(f) = ½ Sφ(f) = kVDD² · Sth / (4π² f²)      (dBc/Hz)

Thus

VCO SSB phase-noise due to the LDO = (kVDD)² · Sth / (4π² foffset²)

How to get kVDD in practice  
• Simulate or measure the oscillator frequency while stepping Vout by a small ΔV:  
 kVDD = (ω0(Vout+ΔV) – ω0(Vout)) / ΔV.  
• Insert that value in the formula above.

Interpretation  
• Because Sth is white, the resulting phase noise falls with 20 dB/dec (1/f²).  
• If you prefer the Hajimiri ISF notation, replace kVDD² with Γvdd,rms²; the final 1/f² form is identical:  
 L(f) = Γvdd,rms² · Sth / (8π² f²).

That is the complete computation of the VCO output phase-noise contribution arising from the LDO’s thermal noise spectrum Sth.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly derives supply-pushing frequency noise, the FM-to-phase conversion, and the 1/f² dependence. It omits the circuit-specific insight that supply perturbations act directly on the varactors, tying Kpush to KVCO and making lower KVCO reduce the noise conversion.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
Voltage noise that appears on the supply rail first produces a small
instantaneous frequency ( “pushing” ) of the oscillator, and the frequency
noise is then integrated by the resonator to become phase noise.

1.  Linearise the dependence of the oscillation frequency on the supply  
    Vout:  
         ω0 (Vout) ≃ ω0,nom + kVDD · (vout – Vout,nom)                (1)  

    kVDD  =  ∂ω0/∂VDD   [rad s-1 V-1] is the supply-pushing coefficient of the
    VCO (it can be measured or obtained from simulation).

2.  The LDO delivers a white thermal-voltage noise with one-sided PSD  
         Svout(f) = Sth   [V²/Hz].

    This noise produces an instantaneous frequency deviation

         δω(t) = kVDD · vout,noise(t)                           (2)

    hence a frequency-noise PSD  

         Sδω(f) = kVDD² · Sth   [rad² s-2 / Hz].               (3)

3.  Phase is the integral of frequency, so in the frequency domain the
    transfer function from frequency to phase is 1/(j2πf).  
    Consequently, the phase-noise PSD is

         Sφ(f) = Sδω(f)/(2πf)²
               = kVDD² · Sth / (2πf)²           [rad²/Hz].      (4)

4.  The single-sideband phase-noise (commonly quoted as L(f) in dBc/Hz) is
    one-half of the two-sided phase-noise PSD:

         L(f) = ½ Sφ(f)
              = kVDD² · Sth / (4π² f²)          [ (radians)²/Hz ]. (5)

    Expressed in dBc/Hz:

         L(f)│dBc/Hz = 10 log₁₀[ kVDD² · Sth / (4π² f²) ].      (6)

Thus, to obtain the VCO output phase noise produced by the LDO’s thermal
noise you need two quantities:

• The supply-pushing coefficient kVDD of the oscillator.  
• The LDO output-noise PSD Sth.

Insert them in eq. (5)/(6); the resulting phase noise falls with 20 dB/dec
(1/f²) from the carrier when the LDO noise is white.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly uses supply pushing to convert LDO noise into frequency noise and applies the 1/f² frequency-to-phase conversion. It omits the circuit-specific insight that the supply perturbation acts on the varactors, so Kpush is closely related to KVCO and lower KVCO reduces this noise conversion.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
Placing the capacitor CT between the tail (node P) and ground makes the tail node an AC-ground at the oscillation frequency and at its harmonics.

1. The 2ω0 common-mode voltage that normally appears at the tail node is therefore highly attenuated.  
2. With that 2ω0 component removed, the low-frequency (1/f) noise of the tail-current source and of the cross-coupled devices can no longer be mixed up to the carrier; the principal up-conversion path is broken.  
3. Consequently, the close-in phase-noise component (the 1/f3 and 1/f2 regions) drops markedly—typically by 10-20 dB once CT is large enough that |1/ j2ω0CT | ≪ r0 of the current source.  
4. The white-noise (far-out) floor, which is set mainly by the tank and the thermal noise of the cross-coupled pair, is almost unchanged.  
5. After CT is large enough to short the tail node at 2ω0, further increase in CT gives little additional benefit.

So, adding CT lowers (improves) the phase noise of the oscillator, especially at frequencies close to the carrier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It predicts a monotonic phase-noise improvement from filtering the tail node, missing the nonmonotonic effect and the class-C improvement and degradation mechanisms.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
Connecting a (large) capacitor CT between the tail node P and ground forces that node to be an a-c ground at the oscillation frequency:

1.  The impedance seen looking into the tail is now 1/(ω0 CT), which can be orders of magnitude smaller than the current-source output resistance ro.  
2.  Therefore the noise current of the tail source (both its white thermal component and, more importantly, its 1/f component) flows almost completely into CT instead of producing a noise voltage at P.  
3.  Because the differential pair senses only the voltage appearing at P, the up-conversion of the tail-source noise to the tank (and hence to phase) is virtually removed.  
4.  With the tail-source contribution suppressed, phase noise is now set mainly by the tank losses and by the channel/shot noise of M1–M2.  Close-in phase noise (the 1/f3 region that was dominated by up-converted flicker noise of the current source) improves typically by 5–15 dB.  
5.  At larger offset frequencies, where the oscillator is already limited by white noise of the core devices and the tank, CT has little effect; the far-out 20-dB/dec (1/f2) slope is almost unchanged.  
6.  The only penalty is a slight reduction of the differential swing because CT adds some extra load, so if CT is made excessively large a small degradation of the far-out noise floor is possible.

In short, placing CT at the tail node markedly lowers the close-in phase noise by shunting the current-source noise away from the LC core.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer claims CT monotonically improves close-in phase noise by shunting tail-source noise. It misses the nonmonotonic effect and the key class-C improvement and possible flicker-noise upconversion, triode operation, or large-CT instability.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
Almost nothing changes.

The noise of the tail-current device that is translated to phase noise is its low-frequency (dc and 1/f) noise.  
That noise is first present around dc, and it is later up-converted by the switching pair to appear as sidebands close to the carrier.  
A capacitor behaves as an ac short only at sufficiently high frequencies; at low frequencies it looks open-circuited.  
Consequently

• At the frequencies that matter for the up-conversion (tens of kilohertz to a few megahertz from dc), CT is practically an open circuit, so the low-frequency noise current of the tail source still flows into the cross-coupled pair and is still mixed to the vicinity of the carrier.  
• Only very-high-frequency components of the tail noise (already far away from the carrier and therefore of little consequence) are shunted to ground by CT.

Hence the close-in phase noise of the oscillator remains essentially the same; adding CT at the tail node does not provide a meaningful phase-noise improvement unless the capacitor is made unrealistically large so that its reactance is small even at the lowest offset frequencies of interest.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer concludes that CT has essentially no effect, missing the nonmonotonic behavior: class-C-like switching can lower phase noise, while flicker-noise upconversion and excessive-CT instability can worsen it. Its tail-source noise-filtering argument does not capture the dominant mechanisms.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
The network of Fig. 17 is nothing more than two identical LC-oscillator cores that are (weakly) cross-coupled so that they start at the same instant and run 90° apart.  
Because the coupling devices carry only a small fraction of the tank current, they do not appreciably modify the resonant impedance of either tank, so the frequency is set almost entirely by the resonance of the inductor L with the total capacitance that appears at each node:

 ωosc ≈ 1 /√(L Ctot)                 fosc ≈ 1 /(2π √(L Ctot))

where  

• L is the value of one side of the centre-tapped spiral, and  
• Ctot is the sum of the intentional tank (or varactor) capacitance and all
device/parasitic capacitances connected to the node (cross-coupled pair,
coupling pair, wiring, pad, etc.).

The mutual coupling only splits the two normal-mode frequencies by a few per-cent,
so the oscillators run practically at the uncoupled resonance:

 feven ≈ f0 (1 + k/2)  fodd ≈ f0 (1 – k/2)        (k ≪ 1)

and the frequency that actually appears at X1–Y1 and X2–Y2 is therefore, to first
order,

 fosc ≈ 1 /(2π √(L Ctot)).

Example  
If L = 3 nH and the total single-ended capacitance is about 2 pF,

 fosc ≈ 1/[2π √(3 nH·2 pF)] ≃ 2.1 GHz.

Thus the circuit oscillates at roughly the LC tank resonance; any deviation caused by the cross-coupling is only a few percent and can usually be neglected in a first-cut estimate.

It instead attributes a small frequency split to mutual inductance and concludes that coupling can be neglected, which misses the circuit’s key frequency-pulling mechanism.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
The two cores in Fig. 17 are ordinary differential LC oscillators that are weakly cross-coupled so that the four outputs are in quadrature.  
The oscillation frequency, therefore, is still set by the resonant frequency of each LC tank:

  ω0 ≈ 1/√(L Ceq)   ⇒  f0 ≈ 1/(2π√(L Ceq))

where Ceq is the total capacitance seen at node X1 (or X2): the varactor capacitance, the intrinsic Cgs/Cgd of the cross-coupled devices, wiring capacitance, etc.

Using the component values normally employed for a 2- to 3-GHz CMOS QVCO,

 • spiral inductor, L ≈ 4 nH  
 • mid-range tank capacitance, Ceq ≈ 1 pF

we obtain

 f0 ≈ 1 / [ 2π √(4 nH × 1 pF) ]  
   ≈ 1 / (2π × 63 ps)  
   ≈ 2.5 GHz.

Hence the circuit of Fig. 17 is expected to oscillate at roughly

 fosc ≃ 2 – 3 GHz (≈ 2.4–2.5 GHz for the above numbers).

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
The network in Fig. 17 in fact contains two identical differential LC tanks that are tied together only to satisfy the 360-deg phase condition; the inter-connections do not appreciably change the reactive impedance seen at the four tank nodes.  
Consequently the oscillation frequency is simply the parallel resonant frequency of one of the tanks.

Let  

 L  = inductance of the spiral in each half–circuit  
 Ctot = total single-ended capacitance appearing at node X1 (or Y1, X2, Y2)

 Ctot = Cvar + Cwire + Cgs + Cgd (of the cross-coupled devices) + other parasitics

Then  

 ω0 ≈ 1 /√(L Ctot)  
 f0 = ω0 /2π ≈ 1 /[2π √(L Ctot)].

Numerical example  
(typical values used in 2- to 3-GHz CMOS LC-VCOs):

 L = 2 nH, Ctot ≈ 2.0–2.5 pF ⟹  

 f0 ≈ 1 /[2π √(2 nH × 2.3 pF)] ≈ 2.3–2.5 GHz.

Thus the circuit will oscillate at approximately  

 f0 ≃ 1 / (2π √(L Ctot)).
